title: Abalūr inscription of Ēkānta Rāmayya
summary: A Kannada stone inscription at Abalūr recording Ēkānta Rāmayya's contest with the Jainas, in which he is said to have offered his own head to Śiva and received it back, and the conversion of the Jaina shrine to Śiva's worship.
notes: The Jaina side is known here only through this Śaiva record (reported by the other side).

title: Abhinavabhāratī (Nāṭyavedavivṛti) of Abhinavagupta
summary: Abhinavagupta's commentary on the Nāṭyaśāstra, the principal source for the debate on how rasa arises: it reports and criticises Lollaṭa, Śaṅkuka and Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka and sets out Abhinava's own view of rasa as the relish (carvaṇā) of a universalized emotion in the spectator's own consciousness, the seven obstacles to it, and śānta as a rasa whose stable basis is knowledge of the self.
notes: Survives with gaps; printed in the Gaekwad's Oriental Series edition of the Nāṭyaśāstra.

title: Abhinavāmṛta
summary: A polemical work by Satyanātha Tīrtha of the Uttarādi Maṭha, called 'the new Amṛta' after Vyāsatīrtha's Nyāyāmṛta; he wrote several works titled 'Abhinava-'.

title: Abhinayadarpaṇa of Nandikeśvara
summary: A short manual of dance and gesture (hand-gestures, glances, head and neck movements) ascribed to Nandikeśvara, basic to classical dance teaching; it states that where the hand goes the eye follows, the mind follows the eye, feeling (bhāva) the mind, and rasa arises from feeling.

title: Abhirāmi Antāti
summary: A Tamil hymn of a hundred verses in antāti form (each verse begins with the last word of the previous) to Abhirāmi, the Goddess of Tirukkaṭavūr, by Abhirāmi Paṭṭar, full of Śrīvidyā imagery.

attribution.tradition: Sung by Abhirāmi Paṭṭar when the Goddess made the full moon appear on a new-moon night to vindicate him before the king
attribution.scholarly: 18th-c. Tamil poem

title: Ācārāṅga Sūtra
summary: The first Aṅga, on the conduct (ācāra) of the mendicant. Book I (Bambhacerāiṃ, 'the discipline of chastity'; nine lectures, the seventh, Mahāparijñā, lost) teaches non-harm to the six classes of living beings (earth, water, fire, plants, mobile beings, wind), detachment and vigilance, and ends with the Upadhānaśruta, the account of Mahāvīra's austerities. Book II (four cūlās) gives detailed rules on alms, lodging, walking, speech, clothing and bowls, and a life of Mahāvīra with the twenty-five bhāvanās of the five great vows.

attribution.tradition: The meaning (artha) was taught by Mahāvīra; the gaṇadhara Sudharman composed the sūtras and transmitted them to Jambū ('suyaṃ me āusaṃ…', 'I have heard, O long-lived one'); redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous compilation with layers of different ages, fixed in writing at Valabhī in the 5th c. CE.

tradition.text: spoken by Mahāvīra and composed by Sudharman

scholarly.text: Book I among the oldest Jain texts (often placed c. 4th–3rd c. BCE); Book II later

structure.description: 2 śrutaskandhas: I = 9 lectures (adhyayana), 44 lessons (uddeśaka), the 7th lecture lost; II = 4 cūlās in 16 lectures (the 5th cūlā became the Niśītha)

summary: Yāmuna's defence of the Vedic authority of the Pāñcarātra. Contrasting it with the 'Māheśvara' tantras, he names four Śaiva groups - Kāpālikas, Kālāmukhas, Pāśupatas and Śaivas - and reports the Kāpālika six insignia and yoni-meditation, the Kālāmukha skull and corpse-ash practices, the Pāśupata five categories, and the claim that initiation makes one a brahmin at once; he judges all of them outside the Veda.

summary: The earliest known text to teach the methods later called haṭha: bindu, identified with the moon in the head, is the essence of life and is consumed by the sun (fire) in the belly; by mahāmudrā, mahābandha and mahāvedha the breath is forced into the central channel, bindu is made steady and the yogin attains the 'nectar of immortality'. It also first teaches the four stages (ārambha, ghaṭa, paricaya, niṣpatti). Its setting is Buddhist tantric, with Śaiva elements.

title: Āpastamba Dharmasūtra
summary: The Dharmasūtra of the Āpastamba Kalpasūtra (praśnas 28–29). It grounds dharma in the agreement of those who know it and in the Vedas (1.1.1.2–3), sets out the four classes and the student's life, contains a chapter on the attainment of the self and the removal of the faults that burn beings through yoga (1.8.22–23), treats the householder, inheritance and the king, lists four orders of life while criticizing the renouncer's claim of liberation by knowledge alone (2.9.21–24), teaches that the classes rise or fall in the next birth by conduct (2.5.11.10–11), and ends that the rest of dharma should be learned from women and from all classes (2.11.29.15).

The Kashmir recension (commented on by Abhinavagupta and Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha) has additional verses and many variant readings. A verse found in some manuscripts (the 'Gītāmāna') speaks of 745 verses (620 by Kṛṣṇa, 57 by Arjuna, 67 by Sañjaya, 1 by Dhṛtarāṣṭra); it is not in the Critical Edition.

summary: Bhakti, with her sons Knowledge and Detachment grown old in the Kali age, is revived by the Bhāgavata; the seven-day hearing surpasses sacrifice, vows, yoga and meditation; the preta Dhundhukārī is freed by hearing it from his brother Gokarṇa.

title: Bhāgavata Purāṇa

attribution.tradition: Composed by Vyāsa, at Nārada's urging, after the Mahābhārata (BhP 1.5-7); taught by Śuka to Parīkṣit on the Gaṅgā during the king's last seven days; retold by the Sūta (Ugraśravas) at Naimiṣa. Given first by the Lord to Brahmā on the lotus (BhP 12.13.10; 2.9 catuḥślokī).
attribution.scholarly: Usually dated c. 9th-10th c. CE and located in the Tamil south, in the milieu of the Āḻvārs; its style is deliberately archaic. Opponents of the text once alleged authorship by the 13th-c. grammarian Vopadeva (see dsp:which-bhagavata-is-the-mahapurana).

tradition.text: Vyāsa's composition at the beginning of the Kali age; recited by Śuka to Parīkṣit

scholarly.text: c. 9th-10th c. CE (some scholars earlier, 6th-8th c.)

structure.description: 12 skandhas, 335 chapters (with variants), 18,000 verses by its own count (BhP 12.13.9)

editions.name: Gita Press Śrīmad Bhāgavata (local e-text, raw_etexts bhAgavata-purANam/wiki)

notes: Commentaries: Śrīdhara Svāmin's Bhāvārthadīpikā (src:bhavarthadipika), Madhva's Bhāgavata-tātparya-nirṇaya, Vīrarāghava, Vijayadhvaja, Vallabha's Subodhinī, Sanātana's Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī, Jīva's Krama-sandarbha, Viśvanātha's Sārārthadarśinī (owned by U13-U16 where they create them). Contains the Kapila Gītā (3.25-33) and Uddhava Gītā (11.7-29), which U06 owns. verse number checked in the local e-text (sanskrit/raw_etexts, bhAgavata-purANam/wiki; Gita Press-type numbering)
summary: The foremost Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa: Kṛṣṇa as Bhagavān himself; bhakti as the supreme dharma; the ten marks; creation, avatāras and cosmography (worlds, Bhū-maṇḍala, hells); the stories of Dhruva, Prahlāda, Ajāmila, Gajendra, Jaḍa Bharata and Ṛṣabha; Kṛṣṇa's life in Vraja with the rāsa-līlā and the gopīs' love in separation (Book 10); the Uddhava Gītā on yoga, powers and devotion; the Kali age, the dissolutions and Śuka's final non-dual teaching.

title: Bhagavatī Sūtra (Vyākhyāprajñapti)
summary: The fifth and largest Aṅga, a vast collection of questions put to Mahāvīra, mostly by Gautama Indrabhūti, on souls, karma, matter, the cosmos, the gods and the path, with narrative sections: the questions of Skandaka and of the laywoman Jayantī, the schism of Jamāli, the followers of Pārśva who accept Mahāvīra, and (śataka 15) the history of Gośāla and his conflict with Mahāvīra. Its answers often distinguish respects (substance, place, time, state), foreshadowing the doctrine of standpoints.

attribution.tradition: The meaning (artha) was taught by Mahāvīra; the gaṇadhara Sudharman composed the sūtras and transmitted them to Jambū ('suyaṃ me āusaṃ…', 'I have heard, O long-lived one'); redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous compilation with layers of different ages, fixed in writing at Valabhī in the 5th c. CE.

tradition.text: the tradition speaks of 36,000 questions answered by Mahāvīra

scholarly.text: a compilation with old and late layers (c. 3rd c. BCE – 5th c. CE)

notes: Pāda themes (per Śaṅkara): 1.1 texts with clear marks of Brahman; 1.2 unclear marks, Brahman as object of meditation; 1.3 unclear marks, Brahman as object of knowledge; 1.4 doubtful words (avyakta, ajā) claimed by Sāṃkhya; 2.1 objections from smṛti (Sāṃkhya, Yoga) and reason answered; 2.2 critique of Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhists, Jains, Pāśupatas and (per Śaṅkara) Pāñcarātra; 2.3 creation of the elements and nature of the jīva; 2.4 the prāṇas; 3.1 transmigration (for dispassion); 3.2 the states of the self and the nature of Brahman; 3.3 combination of meditations; 3.4 auxiliaries of knowledge and the āśramas; 4.1 repetition and the effects of knowledge; 4.2 departure at death; 4.3 the path of the gods; 4.4 the liberated state. All sūtra numbers in this shard follow Śaṅkara's numbering.
summary: Bādarāyaṇa's aphorisms systematizing the Upaniṣads in four adhyāyas — samanvaya (all Upaniṣadic texts converge on Brahman), avirodha (no conflict with smṛti, reason or rival systems, which are critiqued in 2.2), sādhana (transmigration, the states of the self, the meditations, the auxiliaries of knowledge) and phala (repetition of meditation, the knower's freedom from karma, departure, the path of the gods, the liberated state). Every Vedānta school is founded on a commentary on it.

title: Brahmasūtrabhāṣya of Bhāskara (Bhāskarabhāṣya)
summary: Bhāskara's commentary on the Brahma Sūtras: Brahman really transforms into the world through its power; souls are parts of Brahman distinguished by real adjuncts (aupādhika bhedābheda); liberation comes after death through knowledge combined with lifelong ritual duty; it attacks Śaṅkara's doctrine of māyā as Mahāyāna Buddhist in origin.

structure.description: four adhyāyas, each of four pādas, following the sūtras

scholarly.text: c. 8th–9th c. CE (after Śaṅkara, before Vācaspati who answers him)

title: Brahmasūtrabhāṣya (Madhva)

attribution.tradition: Madhva (Ānandatīrtha), counted among his thirty-seven works
attribution.scholarly: accepted as Madhva's

tradition.text: composed by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha); the tradition dates his life to 1199–1278 or 1238–1317

structure.description: 4 adhyāyas × 4 pādas, following Madhva's reading of the sūtras

summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); Madhva's concise commentary on Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtras, reading them as establishing Viṣṇu, full of qualities and free of defects, as the Brahman they inquire into, and as teaching difference, gradation of souls and liberation by grace won through knowledge. It supports its readings with many quotations from Vedic, Pañcarātra and Purāṇic sources.
notes: Opening verse and 1.1.1–1.1.2, 3.1.8, 4.2.16–17, 4.3.10–15, 4.4.19 checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions.

title: Brahmasūtrabhāṣya of Śaṅkara (Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya)

notes: Sub-commentaries: Padmapāda's Pañcapādikā (→ Prakāśātman's Vivaraṇa), Vācaspati's Bhāmatī (→ Amalānanda's Kalpataru → Appayya's Parimala), Ānandagiri's Nyāyanirṇaya, Govindānanda's Ratnaprabhā.
summary: Śaṅkara's commentary on the Brahma Sūtras, opening with the 'adhyāsa-bhāṣya' on superimposition as the root of all empirical dealings; it reads the sūtras as teaching the non-dual Brahman, the unreality of the world apart from Brahman, knowledge alone as the means to liberation, and liberation while living, and it critiques Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, the Buddhist schools, the Jains, the Pāśupatas and the Pāñcarātra.

title: Yādavaprakāśa's commentary on the Brahma Sūtras (lost)
summary: A lost commentary teaching natural (svābhāvika) difference-and-non-difference: Brahman itself transforms into Īśvara, souls and matter. Known from Rāmānuja's Vedārthasaṅgraha and Śrībhāṣya and later Śrīvaiṣṇava refutations.

title: Brahmajāla Sutta
summary: The 'all-embracing net of views': the ethics for which ordinary people praise the Buddha, then the sixty-two grounds on which ascetics and brahmins theorise about the past and the future (eternalism, partial eternalism, finitude, eel-wriggling, chance origin, the self after death, annihilation, nibbāna here and now), all shown to arise from feeling, contact and craving.

title: Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta

structure.description: 28 chapters (GRETIL numbering; Kerala editions with Rudra's Vivaraṇa count 26)

notes: Commentaries: Bhaṭṭotpala (Jagaccandrikā), Rudra (Vivaraṇa, Kerala), Govinda Bhaṭṭatiri (Daśādhyāyī on ch. 1–10).

title: Bṛhat Parāśara Horā Śāstra
summary: A dialogue in which Parāśara teaches Maitreya the horā: creation from Viṣṇu and his three powers, the planets as avatāras of Janārdana who give beings the fruits of karma, planets and signs, the sixteen divisional charts, sign-aspects, the houses, special ascendants, kārakas, yogas, longevity and death-inflicting planets, a great many planetary-period systems (with the Viṃśottarī as chief), aṣṭakavarga, the five great men, renunciation yogas, curses from past births, and a long series of pacificatory rites (śānti) for planets and inauspicious births.

attribution.tradition: taught by the sage Parāśara (father of Vyāsa) to Maitreya
attribution.scholarly: a late compilation; not cited by Varāhamihira or early commentators; printed editions (19th–20th c.) vary widely in content and chapter count

tradition.text: the age of Parāśara, before the Kali age

scholarly.text: compiled in the second millennium CE; received form largely known from 19th–20th c. printed editions

structure.description: 97 chapters in the Sītārām Jhā edition (other editions differ)

notes: Local e-text used for spot checks follows the 97-chapter arrangement.

title: Bṛhat Saṃhitā
summary: Varāhamihira's encyclopaedia of mundane astrology and omens in 106 chapters: the astrologer's qualifications; the courses of sun, moon, Rāhu (with the true cause of eclipses), planets, comets, Agastya and the Seven Seers; the tortoise-division of the land; rain-forecasting; portents (utpāta) and their pacification; bodily signs; site-lore (vāstu), finding water, plants, temples, images and their consecration; animals; the marks of the five great men; gems, pearls, ruby and emerald; perfumes; augury; and the qualities of asterisms, lunar days and karaṇas for action.

structure.description: 106 chapters (Bhat/GRETIL numbering; ch. 5 Rāhucāra, 45 utpāta, 52 vāstu, 53 dakārgala, 55 prāsāda, 57 pratimā, 68 five great men, 79–82 gems, 85–95 śakuna, 97–99 asterism/tithi/karaṇa qualities, 102 marriage, 103 transits)

notes: Commentary: Bhaṭṭotpala (Saṃhitāvivṛti). Local e-text: GRETIL.

title: Bṛhatī

editions.name: Bṛhatī with Ṛjuvimalā, ebhāratī-sampat digital text (ends in adhyāya 6: 'etāvaty eva mātṛkā')

summary: Prabhākara's commentary on Śabara's bhāṣya, the root text of the Prābhākara school; transmitted with Śālikanātha's Ṛjuvimalā. The available text breaks off in the sixth adhyāya.

title: Bṛhatkalpa Bhāṣya
summary: Saṅghadāsagaṇi's large verse commentary on the Bṛhatkalpa, an encyclopedia of monastic casuistry and of social life, completed in Sanskrit by Malayagiri and Kṣemakīrti.

title: Bṛhatkalpa Sūtra
summary: A Chedasūtra stating what is allowed (kappa) and not allowed to monks and nuns — lodgings, food, clothes, bowls, travel, contact between the sexes — including the rule that a nun may not be without clothes; with Saṅghadāsa's bhāṣya and Kṣemakīrti's commentary.

structure.description: 6 uddeśakas

title: Bṛhatkhecarīprakāśa

attribution.tradition: by Ballāla
attribution.scholarly: a 17th–18th c. commentary on the Khecarīvidyā used in Mallinson's edition (recalled)

summary: A long commentary on the Khecarīvidyā that quotes many earlier yoga texts. RESTRICTED subject matter; summary only.

title: Bṛhaṭṭīkā (lost)
notes: Its scope (a longer treatment of the tarkapāda?) and which later quotations derive from it are uncertain; verses on omniscience quoted in Buddhist and Jain works are sometimes assigned to it.
summary: A lost larger work of Kumārila, known through later quotations and references.

title: Buddhavaṃsa
summary: The chronicle of the Buddhas: the ascetic Sumedha's vow at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara to become a Buddha, and the lives of the twenty-four Buddhas who followed up to Gotama.

structure.description: 28 chapters (the 25 Buddhas from Dīpaṅkara to Gotama, plus the jewel-walk, the other Buddhas and the distribution of relics)

title: Caitanya Bhāgavata
summary: Vṛndāvana Dāsa's Bengali biography of Caitanya (originally titled Caitanya Maṅgala), rich on the Navadvīpa period, the nocturnal kīrtanas and Nityānanda; in three khaṇḍas (Ādi, Madhya, Antya).

structure.description: Ādi, Madhya and Antya khaṇḍas

title: Caitanyacandrodaya
summary: Kavikarṇapūra's ten-act Sanskrit drama on Caitanya's life (1572 CE per tradition).

title: Caitanya Caritāmṛta
summary: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja's Bengali verse biography and theology of Caitanya, interspersed with Sanskrit verses, in three parts: Ādi (17 chapters), Madhya (25) and Antya (20). It sets out who Caitanya is (Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā's mood), his teachings to Rūpa, Sanātana, Rāmānanda, Sārvabhauma and Prakāśānanda, and his last years of divine madness at Purī.

structure.description: 3 līlās: Ādi 17, Madhya 25, Antya 20 chapters (cited here as 1.x.y, 2.x.y, 3.x.y)

scholarly.text: completed c. 1612–1615 CE (one colophon reading gives 1615; an alternative reading 1581)

title: Caitanya Maṅgala (of Jayānanda)
summary: Jayānanda's Bengali biography of Caitanya, notable for an account of his death.

title: Caitanya Maṅgala (of Locana Dāsa)
summary: Locana Dāsa's Bengali song-biography of Caitanya, based on Murāri Gupta.

title: Caitanya Upaniṣad
summary: A text presented as part of the Atharvaveda that describes Caitanya as the Lord's appearance in Kali; published with a commentary by Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura in the late 19th c.

tradition.text: Part of the Atharvaveda

scholarly.text: Late; first attested in 19th-c. Gauḍīya publication

title: Cakkavatti-sīhanāda Sutta
summary: Be an island to yourselves, roaming in your own pasture (the four satipaṭṭhānas); the tale of the wheel-turning kings, the decline of human lifespan through the neglect of Dhamma, its renewal, and the coming of the Buddha Metteyya.

editions.name: Mahāsaṅgīti Tipiṭaka Buddhavasse 2500 (World Tipiṭaka edition, based on the Sixth Council text), as published by SuttaCentral in bilara-data (root/pli/ms); local copy in sources_raw/bilara-data
editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

editions.name: Bhikkhu Sujato (English), SuttaCentral

notes: SuttaCentral uid dn26; Mahāsaṅgīti title 'Cakkavattisutta' (checked locally).

title: Cakradatta (Cikitsāsaṅgraha)
summary: A therapeutic compendium by Cakrapāṇidatta, arranged by disease, much used in Bengal.

title: Camakam (Camaka-praśna)
summary: The Yajurveda litany that follows the Śatarudrīya: a long series of petitions 'and … for me' (… ca me) — food and impulse, the breaths, mind, speech, eye and ear, strength and life, truth and faith, well-being, the Vedic rites and their implements, and finally the numbers — each to be made fit by the sacrifice (yajñena kalpantām).
notes: Recited with the Śatarudrīya (Namakam-Camakam); ritually the formulas accompany the 'stream of wealth' (vasordhārā) offering of the agnicayana (moderate confidence).

checks.note: TS 4.7.1–11 (vājaś ca me … to the numbers) and VS 18.1–27 (ending 'yajñena kalpantām') located. Vasordhārā as the agnicayana libation with these formulas confirmed at general level (Hindupedia: 'stream of wealth' at the agnicayana, mantras from TS and VS).

title: Camatkāracintāmaṇi
summary: Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa's short verses on the results of planets in the houses.

title: Caṇḍamāruta
summary: Doḍḍayācārya's commentary on Deśika's Śatadūṣaṇī, continuing the polemic against Advaita.

title: Caṇḍīdās padāvalī
summary: Lyrics on Rādhā's love and separation signed 'Caṇḍīdās' (the name of more than one poet), sung by Caitanya and later claimed by the Sahajiyās.

attribution.tradition: One Caṇḍīdās of Nānnur, lover of Rāmī the washerwoman.
attribution.scholarly: Several poets (Baḍu, Dvija, Dīna Caṇḍīdās); attributions unresolved.

title: Rāgātmikā padas of the Sahajiyā Caṇḍīdās

attribution.tradition: songs of Caṇḍīdās, lover of the washerwoman Rāmī
attribution.scholarly: the 'Caṇḍīdās problem': several poets used the name (Baḍu Caṇḍīdās of the Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtan, Dvija and Dīna Caṇḍīdās); the Sahajiyā padas are generally later

tradition.text: the tradition places Caṇḍīdās before Caitanya (who is said to have enjoyed his songs)

summary: The songs ascribed to the Sahajiyā Caṇḍīdās: 'Listen, brother man — the truth of man is above all, nothing is above it'; everyone speaks of sahaja but who knows it?; the washerwoman's love is tested gold without a trace of lust.
notes: Distinct from src:candidas-padavali (U26), the general Caṇḍīdās pada collection; this id gathers the Sahajiyā (rāgātmikā) songs.

title: Caṇḍīmaṅgala (Mukundarām Cakravartī)
summary: The best-known Bengali 'auspicious poem' of the Goddess Caṇḍī, telling of her grace to the hunter Kālaketu and the merchant Dhanapati and his son Śrīmanta; a narrative source for popular Śākta devotion in Bengal.

title: Candraprajñapti (Candapaṇṇatti)
summary: Jain canonical upāṅga on the moon's course, nearly identical in content to the Sūryaprajñapti.

title: Cāndra-vyākaraṇa
summary: Candragomin's grammar, closely based on Pāṇini but without Vedic rules and accents, transmitted especially in Buddhist circles (Nepal, Tibet, Sri Lanka).

title: Candrajñānāgama

attribution.tradition: revealed by Sadāśiva from the upper (Īśāna) face; first received by Ananta, then Bṛhaspati (Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92; Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10)
attribution.scholarly: texts now transmitted under this title are mostly South Indian redactions centred on temple ritual; their relation to the early scripture of the same name is not established here

structure.description: Rudrabheda no. 19 in the Kāmika's order; 14 upabhedas in the Kāmika's list

editions.name: Muktabodha M00263, M00273 (the latter describes itself as a pratiṣṭhātantra); Vīraśaiva recension M00201

notes: Kiraṇa 10.16/10.23: 'Candrabhāsa' of Ananta → the gods' priest (Bṛhaspati). Śrīkaṇṭhīya: 'Candrāṃśu'. In the Kāmika's image of the scriptures as Sadāśiva's body it is the chest (pūrva 1.93–101). Lists checked by the Phase-B author against local e-texts: Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/Kamikagama.md (Kāmika Pūrvabhāga, Madras 1909 Grantha ed. as transcribed)), Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10.3–27 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/kiranagama.md (Kiraṇa vidyāpāda, South Indian printed text as transcribed)) and the Śrīkaṇṭhīya list quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)).
summary: No. 19 of the 28 Śaiva Siddhānta mūlāgamas (Rudrabheda). According to the Kāmika it was first received by Ananta, then Bṛhaspati. The Kāmika assigns it 14 upabheda(s): Sthira, Sthāṇu, Mahānta, Vāruṇa, Nandikeśvara, Ekapādapurāṇa, Śaṅkara, Nīlarudraka, Śivabhadra, Kalpabheda, Śrīmukha, Śivaśāsana, Śivaśekhara, Devyāmata. A 'Candrajñāna' also appears in the Vāmakeśvara's list of 64 tantras.

title: Candrajñānāgama (Vīraśaiva recension)
summary: The Vīraśaiva recension of the Candrajñāna Āgama (kriyā- and caryā-pāda), one of the Āgamas the tradition reads as teaching Vīraśaiva dharma in its later portion.

editions.name: Muktabodha digital library e-text M00201

notes: Distinct from the Śaiva Siddhānta transmission of the Candrajñāna (U08).

title: Candrakalā Nāḍī (Deva Keralam)
summary: A Sanskrit nāḍī text on the divisions of the signs and their results, printed in the 20th century.

title: Candraprajñapti
summary: An Upāṅga on the moon's course and calendar, nearly identical with the Sūryaprajñapti apart from its opening.

title: Candrāvalokana
summary: A short dialogue in which Maheśvara instructs Matsyendra on the śāmbhavī seal (inner aim, outer unwinking gaze), the dissolution of breath and mind, the 'new-moon, first-day and full-moon' of the eyes, desire (kāma), poison (viṣa) and the spotless (nirañjana), the mind as the seed from which bindu arises, and the six centres.

editions.name: Muktabodha e-text M00506 ('Candrāvalocakana')

notes: Several verses are shared with the Haṭhapradīpikā (e.g. the verse ending 'dambha-mithyā-pralāpaḥ' = HYP 4.114). Date unknown.

title: Candravedhyaka
summary: A Prakīrṇaka counted in some lists: on the qualities of teacher and pupil, discipline and concentration at death, with the image of the archer who must pierce the eye of a revolving doll (candravedhya) as a figure for unwavering attention.

title: Candrikāprakāśa

tradition.text: Rāghavendra entered his brindāvana at Mantrālaya in 1671

summary: Rāghavendra Tīrtha's commentary on Vyāsatīrtha's Tātparyacandrikā.

title: Cāṅgadeva Pāsaṣṭī
summary: Jñāneśvar's letter of sixty-five ovīs to the aged yogī Cāṅgadev: the self is one, like gold in all ornaments; knower, knowing and known are one reality; addressing it as 'you' or 'I' already divides it.

attribution.tradition: Cāṅgadev, unable to decide how to address the boy-sage, sent a blank letter; Muktābāī remarked that after fourteen hundred years he was still blank, and Jñāneśvar answered in 65 ovīs.
attribution.scholarly: Generally accepted as Jñāneśvar's.

structure.description: 65 ovīs ('pāsaṣṭ' = sixty-five)

title: Caṅkaṟpa Nirākaraṇam
summary: Umāpati's refutation of nine views close to the Siddhānta — Māyāvāda, Aikyavāda, Pāṣāṇavāda, Bhedavāda, Śivasamavāda, Saṅkrāntavāda, Īśvarāvikāravāda, Nimittakāraṇapariṇāmavāda and Śivādvaita — especially on the relation of the freed soul to Śiva.
notes: The list of nine is given at moderate confidence.

title: Caraka Saṃhitā

attribution.tradition: The teaching of Punarvasu Ātreya set down by his disciple Agniveśa, redacted (pratisaṃskṛta) by Caraka and completed by Dṛḍhabala of Pañcanada, who supplied seventeen chapters of the Cikitsā and the Kalpa and Siddhi sections (Ca Si 12.36-40); Caraka is a partial incarnation of Śeṣa (Bhāvaprakāśa).
attribution.scholarly: A layered text: an older Agniveśa core, Caraka's redaction and Dṛḍhabala's supplement (c. 4th–5th c. CE).

tradition.text: Ātreya's teaching at the assembly of sages in the Himalaya, in a former age

scholarly.text: Caraka's redaction c. 1st c. BCE – 2nd c. CE; Dṛḍhabala c. 4th–5th c. CE

structure.description: Eight sthānas, 120 chapters (Ca Sū 30.33): Sūtra/Śloka 30, Nidāna 8, Vimāna 8, Śārīra 8, Indriya 12, Cikitsā 30, Kalpa 12, Siddhi 12

summary: The foundational compendium of internal medicine: Ātreya's teaching to Agniveśa in dialogues and assemblies of sages. It sets out the aim and definition of Āyurveda, the doṣas, dhātus and malas, diet, daily and seasonal routine and good conduct, the causes and diagnosis of disease, the examination of patient and physician, debate, the person and its constituents, embryology, the signs of death, therapeutics including rejuvenation and virility, and purificatory therapies; and it teaches a doctrine of the self, rebirth, yoga and liberation (Sū 11; Śā 1, 5).

editions.name: ed. Jādavji Trikamji Ācārya with Cakrapāṇi's Āyurvedadīpikā (Bombay, Nirnaya Sagar 1941 and reprints)
DCS e-text (local copy in sources_raw/dcs)

notes: Refs in this unit: sthāna abbreviation + chapter.verse (su = Sūtra, ni = Nidāna, vi = Vimāna, sa = Śārīra, in = Indriya, ci = Cikitsā, ka = Kalpa, si = Siddhi); Ci 1 has four pādas (ci.1.4.30 = Cikitsā 1, pāda 4, verse 30).

title: Carakanyāsa
summary: Bhaṭṭāra Haricandra's early commentary on the Caraka Saṃhitā, known from fragments and citations.

title: Carakatattvapradīpikā
summary: Śivadāsa Sena's commentary on the Caraka Saṃhitā (15th c.).

title: Caraṇavyūha
summary: A short treatise listing the branches (śākhās, caraṇas) of the four Vedas and their extent — e.g. the five Ṛgveda śākhās (Śākala, Bāṣkala, Āśvalāyana, Śāṅkhāyana, Māṇḍūkāyana) — ascribed to Śaunaka or Kātyāyana; the Atharvaveda has its own Caraṇavyūha among its Pariśiṣṭas.

attribution.tradition: Śaunaka (or Kātyāyana)
attribution.scholarly: late compilation; its counts of śākhās are traditional

notes: Ascription and exact lists recalled from memory; to be checked.

checks.note: Confirmed: 'Śaunaka's Caraṇavyūha' names five Ṛgveda śākhās — Śākala, Bāṣkala, Āśvalāyana, Śāṅkhāyana, Māṇḍūkāyana (edition with Mahidāsa's commentary). The alternative ascription to Kātyāyana was not confirmed. The Atharvaveda's own Caraṇavyūha (AVPariś 49) is located locally; note that it lists SEVEN Ṛgveda śākhās (āśvalāyana, śāṅkhāyana, sādhyāyana, śākala, bāṣkala, audumbara, māṇḍūka), so 'five' applies only to Śaunaka's text.

alt_summary: A short supplement (pariśiṣṭa) listing the branches (śākhā) of the four Vedas and the auxiliary sciences, including the four Upavedas — medicine (āyurveda), archery/warfare (dhanurveda), music (gāndharvaveda) and statecraft/architecture — attached to the four Vedas.
alt_notes: The assignment of the fourth Upaveda (arthaśāstra or sthāpatyaveda) varies between sources; attribution (Śaunaka?) not asserted.

title: Cariyāpiṭaka
summary: 35 verse accounts of the Buddha's former lives illustrating the fulfilment of the perfections (pāramī) — giving, virtue, renunciation, determination, truthfulness, loving-kindness and equanimity.

structure.description: 3 vaggas, 35 stories (only seven of the ten perfections are illustrated)

title: Caṭakōpar Antāti
summary: A hundred-verse antāti in praise of Nammāḻvār (Caṭakōpaṉ) attributed to Kampaṉ.

scholarly.text: c. 12th c. CE if by Kampaṉ

notes: Attribution to Kampaṉ is the tradition's; tradition says he composed it so that his Rāmāyaṇa would be accepted at Śrīraṅgam. Verse count as recalled.

title: Catuḥśaraṇa Prakīrṇaka
summary: A short Prakīrṇaka on taking the four refuges — the Arhats, the Siddhas, the monks and the dharma taught by the omniscient — with confession of wrongs and approval of good deeds.

title: Catuḥślokī
summary: Yāmuna's four verses in praise of Śrī (Lakṣmī), declaring that even the Lord cannot measure her greatness and that she is the Lord's consort, whose servants are all the gods; later the Vaṭakalai cite it for Śrī's supremacy.

tradition.text: Yāmuna, 916–1041 CE in one traditional reckoning

title: Catuḥślokī Bhāgavata (of Eknāth)
summary: Eknāth's Marathi ovī commentary on the four 'seed' verses of the Bhāgavata (2.9.32–35), in which the Lord teaches Brahmā that he alone was before creation and remains after it.

attribution.tradition: Eknāth's.
attribution.scholarly: Accepted.

title: Catuḥślokī (of Vallabha)
summary: Four verses redefining the four aims of life for the devotee: dharma is always serving the Lord of Vraja with one's whole being.

title: Caturdaṇḍīprakāśikā of Veṅkaṭamakhin
summary: Veṅkaṭamakhin's treatise that sets out the scheme of seventy-two parent scales (melakarta), the basis of later Karṇāṭaka rāga classification.

title: Caturvargacintāmaṇi

attribution.tradition: Hemādri's 'wish-gem of the four aims'.
attribution.scholarly: A 13th-c. Yādava-court digest; its Vrata-khaṇḍa and Dāna-khaṇḍa collect Purāṇic vrata and dāna teaching.

summary: An encyclopedic digest of vows, gifts, times and rites, drawn largely from the Purāṇas.
alt_summary: Hemādri's vast digest on the four aims of life, of which the parts on vows (vrata), gifts (dāna), pilgrimage, śrāddha and the division of time survive.

title: Cauppannamahāpurisacariya
summary: Śīlāṅka (Śīlācārya)'s Prakrit prose-and-verse history of the fifty-four 'great men' (the sixty-three less the nine prativāsudevas, who are treated with their vāsudevas).
notes: Whether this Śīlāṅka is the Ācārāṅga commentator is debated.

title: Caurāsī Vaiṣṇavan kī Vārtā
summary: Braj Bhāṣā prose accounts of eighty-four disciples of Vallabha (including Sūrdās, Kumbhandās, Paramānanddās and Kṛṣṇadās), attributed to Gokulnāth, with Harirāy's commentary Bhāvaprakāś.

scholarly.text: 17th c. CE in its present form

title: Cēkkiḻār Purāṇam
summary: A verse life of Cēkkiḻār attributed to Umāpati Civācāriyār: his ministry under the Cōḻa king and the composition of the Periya Purāṇam.

title: Vacanas of Cennabasava
summary: Vacanas signed Kūḍalacennasaṅgamadēva, honoured in the tradition for their systematic exposition of the ṣaṭsthala path, the relation of liṅga and aṅga, and the eight shields (aṣṭāvaraṇa).

structure.description: among the largest single-author collections (count not recalled reliably)

notes: aṅkita (signature): Kūḍalacennasaṅgamadēva. Cited by incipit; edition numbering to be fixed in Phase D.

title: Chāgaleya Upaniṣad

attribution.tradition: śruti
attribution.scholarly: edited by S. K. Belvalkar (1925) (moderate confidence)

structure.description: a short prose text

summary: A short prose Upaniṣad using the image of the chariot and charioteer for the body and the self (low confidence on contents).

editions.name: Sanskrit text with Śaṅkara's bhasya (Advaita-Sarada e-text; GitHub sanskrit/raw_etexts mirror)
editions.licence: public domain text; e-text licence per repository

notes: Veda affiliation: uncertain

title: Chāndogya Upaniṣad

attribution.tradition: śruti, 'seen' by the sages whose teaching it records; not a human composition
attribution.scholarly: anonymous compilation within the Vedic schools (śākhās), incorporating older materials

tradition.text: Revealed scripture (śruti): in the Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta view without human author and beginningless; the texts themselves trace their teaching through lineages of teachers back to Brahma/Prajāpati and brahman, the self-existent

scholarly.text: c. 7th-6th c. BCE (rough estimate; with BAU the oldest)

structure.description: 8 prapathakas (chapters), about 154 khandas, mainly prose (Śaṅkara's text numbers ch.kh.verse)

summary: One of the two oldest and largest Upanisads: meditations on the udgītha and Om; the honey of the sun; Śāṇḍilya's teaching that all this is brahman and the self in the heart is brahman; Raikva, Satyakāma Jābāla and Upakosala; the contest of the breaths; the five fires and the two paths; Aśvapati's vaiśvānara self; Uddalaka's teaching to Śvetaketu of being (sat) with its refrain tat tvam asi; Sanatkumāra's ladder to plenitude (bhūman); the small space in the heart; Prajāpati's teaching to Indra and Virocana.

editions.name: Sanskrit text with Śaṅkara's bhasya (Advaita-Sarada e-text; GitHub sanskrit/raw_etexts mirror)
editions.licence: public domain text; e-text licence per repository

editions.name: R. E. Hume, The Thirteen Principal Upanishads (1921)
F. Max Muller, The Upanishads, SBE 1 and 15 (1879, 1884)

notes: Forms prapathakas 3-10 of the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa, whose first two prapathakas are the Mantra Brāhmaṇa (src:mantra-brahmana, U02) (moderate confidence). Veda affiliation: Sāmaveda, Kauthuma-Ranayaniya tradition

title: Chāndogyopaniṣad-bhāṣya (Madhva)

attribution.tradition: Madhva (Ānandatīrtha), counted among his thirty-seven works
attribution.scholarly: accepted as Madhva's

tradition.text: composed by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha); the tradition dates his life to 1199–1278 or 1238–1317

summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); Madhva's commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, reading it as teaching Viṣṇu's supremacy and his difference from souls and matter, often by etymological explanation of names and by quotations from other scriptures. On 6.8.7 it glosses 'aitadātmya' as being under the Lord's control and warns against the conceit of identity with Viṣṇu.
notes: checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions

title: Chāndogyopaniṣadbhāṣya of Śaṅkara
summary: Śaṅkara's commentary on the Chāndogya, including the teaching of Uddālaka ('tat tvam asi', ch. 6), the bhūman (ch. 7) and the self of Prajāpati's instruction (ch. 8), and its many meditations (upāsanā).

title: Chummāsaṅketaprakāśa
summary: A Krama work on the coded instructions (chummā) of the tradition, ascribed to Niṣkriyānandanātha.
notes: Recalled from secondary literature; verify in Phase C. 'Chummā' as Kaula code-word is attested at TĀ 4.268.

title: Cidgaganacandrikā
summary: A Krama-inspired hymn/treatise on the Kālīs of consciousness by Śrīvatsa (called Kālidāsa).

editions.name: Tantrik Texts series (1937) - catalogue data

title: Cidvallī
summary: Naṭanānandanātha's commentary on the Kāmakalāvilāsa, explaining the verses through Pratyabhijñā and Śrīvidyā doctrine (e.g. Tripurā as 'she who existed before the three lights').

title: Cihna-yātrā
summary: Śaṅkaradeva's first dramatic performance, staged with painted scenes of the seven Vaikuṇṭhas; the text is lost. Performed as bhāonā with a sūtradhāra who sings, dances and explains.

attribution.tradition: Śaṅkaradeva's.
attribution.scholarly: Accepted.

title: Cikitsākalikā
summary: Tīsaṭa's short verse manual of therapeutics.

title: Ciñciṇīmatasārasamuccaya
summary: A Kubjikā compendium from Nepal summarising the Paścimāmnāya's teachings on the Goddess and the transmission.
notes: Recalled from secondary literature (Dyczkowski); verify.

title: Cintra praśasti (1287 CE)

title: Cintyāgama
alt_titles: Acintyaviśvasādākhya (title of a surviving text; relation uncertain)

attribution.tradition: revealed by Sadāśiva from the upper (Īśāna) face; first received by (Su)dīpta, then Gopati, then Ambikā (Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92; Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10)
attribution.scholarly: texts now transmitted under this title are mostly South Indian redactions centred on temple ritual; their relation to the early scripture of the same name is not established here

structure.description: Śivabheda no. 3 in the Kāmika's order; 6 upabhedas in the Kāmika's list

editions.name: Acintyaviśvasādākhya (Muktabodha M00272) — relation to the Cintya not established here

notes: Kiraṇa 10.4/10.8: 'Acintya' to Dīpta; Dīptarudra → Gopati → Ambikā. Śrīkaṇṭhīya: 'Cintya'. In the Kāmika's image of the scriptures as Sadāśiva's body it is the toes (pūrva 1.93–101). Lists checked by the Phase-B author against local e-texts: Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/Kamikagama.md (Kāmika Pūrvabhāga, Madras 1909 Grantha ed. as transcribed)), Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10.3–27 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/kiranagama.md (Kiraṇa vidyāpāda, South Indian printed text as transcribed)) and the Śrīkaṇṭhīya list quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)).
summary: No. 3 of the 28 Śaiva Siddhānta mūlāgamas (Śivabheda). According to the Kāmika it was first received by (Su)dīpta, then Gopati, then Ambikā. The Kāmika assigns it 6 upabheda(s): Sucintya, Subhaga, Vāma, Pāpanāśa, Parodbhava, Amṛta. No complete text securely identified with the Cintya is recorded here.

title: Ciṟiya Tirumaṭal
summary: Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār's shorter maṭal poem: Parakāla-nāyakī, spurned by the Lord, threatens to 'ride the maṭal' (the palmyra-stem horse) through the streets to shame him — a threat that Tamil convention allowed only to men.

scholarly.text: c. 8th c. CE (praises the Pallava Nandivarman II Pallavamalla, r. c. 731–796)

title: Cittā vaittiyat tiraṭṭu (compendium of Siddha medicine)

notes: Compiler and date not recalled; possibly a 20th-c. compilation (then recent).

title: Civañāṉa Māpāṭiyam

title: Civañāṉa Pōtac Ciṟṟurai
summary: Civañāṉa Muṉivar's short commentary on the Civañāṉa Pōtam, the standard teaching gloss.

attribution.tradition: Cokhāmeḷā's; Nāmdev's circle preserved them.
attribution.scholarly: Traditional attribution; some songs are later.

tradition.text: Cokhāmeḷā died c. 1338

scholarly.text: Scholarly accounts differ by text. Several Yoga Upaniṣads (e.g. Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kṣurikā, Tejobindu, Nādabindu, Dhyānabindu, Brahmavidyā, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā, Haṃsa) survive in shorter northern versions that are older; the expanded southern recensions (as in this collection) borrow from medieval haṭha works and were probably compiled in South India, perhaps as late as the 18th c. (Bouy 1994).

summary: Dattātreya (Viṣṇu) teaches Sāṅkṛti eight-limbed yoga in ten sections: ten yamas and niyamas with inner meanings, postures, channels, winds, inner time and inner tīrthas, purification, breath-control, five withdrawals, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi as knowledge of identity.

title: Daśāśrutaskandha
summary: A Chedasūtra in ten chapters: the twenty faults disturbing concentration (asamādhi-sthāna), the twenty-one grave faults (śabala), the thirty-three disrespects to the teacher (āśātanā), the eight accomplishments of a gaṇin, the ten states of mental concentration, the eleven stages of the layman (upāsaka-pratimā), the twelve special vows of the monk (bhikṣu-pratimā), the Paryuṣaṇākalpa (the Kalpa Sūtra), the thirty sources of deluding karma, and the nine kinds of 'wishing for a reward' (nidāna).

summary: The first text to teach a system it calls haṭhayoga. Dattātreya names four yogas — mantra, laya, haṭha and rāja (the best) — and four stages; he teaches the eight-limbed yoga 'known to Yājñavalkya and others' and the haṭha of 'Kapila and the others' (mahāmudrā, mahābandha, mahāvedha, khecarī, the three bandhas, viparītakaraṇī, vajrolī with amarolī and sahajolī). tradition.text: part of Vyāsa's Mārkaṇḍeya

structure.description: 13 chapters in three caritas (ch. 1; chs. 2-4; chs. 5-13). The tradition counts 700 mantras (hence 'Saptaśatī') by counting half-verses, speaker-lines and refrains; the metrical verses number c. 580-590 (588 numbered verses in the Sansknet e-text)

notes: Recited with ancillary texts (aṅgas): Kavaca, Argalā, Kīlaka before, and the three Rahasyas (Prādhānika, Vaikṛtika, Mūrti) after; the naming of the three caritas' deities as Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī comes from the dhyāna verses and the Rahasyas, not from the 13 chapters themselves. Commentaries include Bhāskararāya's Guptavatī (src:guptavati) and the Śāntanavī. Śākta theology shared with U23. verse number checked in the GRETIL/Sansknet e-text of the MkP (chs. 1-93; Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81-93 in this numbering)
summary: The Goddess, Mahāmāyā, is the eternal source and power of the world who deludes even the wise and grants liberation; she wakes Viṣṇu to slay Madhu and Kaiṭabha, arises from the gods' combined radiance to slay Mahiṣa, and as Ambikā with Kālī/Cāmuṇḍā and the Mothers slays Śumbha, Niśumbha and their generals; hymned as present in all beings ('yā devī sarvabhūteṣu'), she promises to return whenever demons oppress the world.

title: Dṛṣṭivāda
summary: The twelfth Aṅga, lost according to both traditions. As described in the Nandī and Samavāyāṅga it had five parts — parikarma, sūtra, pūrvagata (the fourteen Pūrvas), anuyoga (including the first narrative anuyoga) and cūlikā — and contained all doctrine. The Digambaras hold that portions of two Pūrvas survive in the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa.

attribution.tradition: Composed by the gaṇadharas; the fourteen Pūrvas were known in full last by the śrutakevalin Bhadrabāhu; Sthūlabhadra learned the last four as text only; knowledge of the Pūrvas died out gradually (Śvetāmbara: with Devarddhigaṇi's time; Digambara: within 683 years of the nirvāṇa).

structure.description: 5 parts; the pūrvagata comprised 14 Pūrvas (see cpt:fourteen-purvas)

summary: The oldest extant complete commentary on the Gītā. title: Gīta Govinda
summary: Jayadeva's Sanskrit song-poem in twelve cantos and twenty-four songs (aṣṭapadīs, each set to a named rāga and tāla) with linking verses: Kṛṣṇa's spring dance with the cowherd women, Rādhā's jealousy and withdrawal, the longing of both in separation carried by Rādhā's friend, Kṛṣṇa's plea for forgiveness, and their union. It opens with a hymn to the ten avatāras borne by Kṛṣṇa and offers itself to those whose minds delight in remembering Hari and in the arts of love.

attribution.tradition: Composed by Jayadeva, son of Bhojadeva and Rāmādevī (as the closing verse says), in the service of Jagannātha at Purī (Odisha account) or at the Bengal court of Lakṣmaṇasena (Bengal account); by tradition Kṛṣṇa himself wrote one line (10th canto).
attribution.scholarly: Jayadeva, 12th c. CE; the opening names poets of Lakṣmaṇasena's court (Umāpatidhara, Śaraṇa, Govardhana, Dhoyī); his birthplace (Kenduli in Bengal or Kenduli Sasan in Odisha, or Mithilā) is disputed.

structure.description: 12 sargas (cantos) with 24 aṣṭapadī songs and interspersed ślokas; canto titles as commonly printed: Sāmoda-dāmodara, Akleśa-keśava, Mugdha-madhusūdana, Snigdha-madhusūdana, Sākāṅkṣa-puṇḍarīkākṣa, Dhṛṣṭa-vaikuṇṭha, Nāgara-nārāyaṇa, Vilakṣa-lakṣmīpati, Mugdha-mukunda, Catura-caturbhuja, Sānanda-dāmodara, Suprīta-pītāmbara (variants exist)

notes: Liturgical use: sung daily before Jagannātha at Purī (by tradition confirmed by an order of Gajapati Pratāparudra, c. 1499, that the temple singers sing only the Gīta Govinda — recalled with moderate confidence); sung in Kerala temples as aṣṭapadī (sopāna saṅgītam) and in South Indian bhajana; relished by Caitanya (Caitanya Caritāmṛta); two of Jayadeva's hymns (not from the Gīta Govinda) are in the Sikh Ādi Granth (context only). Canto-title list: moderate/low confidence. Not to be confused with the later Jayadeva (Pīyūṣavarṣa) of the Candrāloka and Prasannarāghava.

attribution.tradition: written at Galta (Jaipur) at Govindadeva's command in a dream, to establish the Gauḍīyas' own Brahma Sūtra commentary

title: Govindalīlāmṛta

title: Govindaprabhu-caritra (Ṛddhipur-caritra)

title: Grahacāranibandhana (Parahita system)

title: Grahalāghava

title: Grāmageya-gāna (Veyagāna)
summary: The first song-book of the Kauthuma–Rāṇāyanīya Sāmaveda: the melodies on the Pūrvārcika verses 'to be sung in the village', i.e. in public ritual; it shows how each verse is transformed into a sāman with stretched vowels, repetitions and stobhas.

title: Gūḍhārthadīpikā
summary: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā, reading its three hexads as the sections on works, devotion/meditation and knowledge, and joining Advaita with an intense devotion to Kṛṣṇa.

checks.note: Extant and digitized. Scholarly estimates for Madhusūdana range c. 1490–1632 (Wikipedia gives c. 1490–1580); the entry's 16th–17th c. (1540–1650) overlaps these; the upper bound may be slightly late.

alt_summary: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaita commentary on the Gītā, which also exalts devotion; it divides the Gītā into three sections of six chapters — action, devotion (upāsanā) and knowledge — corresponding to the three parts of the Veda and to the words 'thou', 'that' and 'art' of the great saying.

Without knowing the guru-principle, sacrifices, vows and pilgrimages are fruitless; the teaching is secret and to be given only to the devoted.

tradition.text: Śruti: eternal and authorless; no human date

scholarly.text: Scholarly accounts differ by text. Several Yoga Upaniṣads (e.g. Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kṣurikā, Tejobindu, Nādabindu, Dhyānabindu, Brahmavidyā, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā, Haṃsa) survive in shorter northern versions that are older; the expanded southern recensions (as in this collection) borrow from medieval haṭha works and were probably compiled in South India, perhaps as late as the 18th c. (Bouy 1994).

summary: Gautama asks Sanatsujāta (in this recension) for the knowledge Śiva gave Pārvatī: the haṃsa (the self as the natural breath-mantra haṃsa/so'ham) pervading all bodies, its ascent through the centres, the mantra's seer, metre and deity, the eight-petalled heart lotus whose directions govern moods, and the ten inner sounds with their effects, ending in becoming Brahman.

summary: One of the three gems of the Pāñcarātra, in 33 paṭalas. Sages ask Śāṇḍilya, who relates Bhagavān's teaching to Nārada. It distinguishes Brahmā's, primordial matter's and the pure creation (paṭalas 2–4), and treats mantras, initiation, worship, meditation and yoga (paṭala 33). An additional passage in the printed text names the three gems and their expansions (Pādma, Pārameśvara, Īśvara) and assigns them to Kāñcī, Śrīraṅgam and Melkote.

title: Kāvyādarśa of Daṇḍin
summary: Daṇḍin's 'mirror of poetry' in three chapters: the body of poetry, the southern (vaidarbha) and eastern (gauḍa) styles and their ten qualities, and the figures of sense and sound. Its opening praises the light called word, without which the three worlds would be blind darkness.

title: Kāvyakautuka of Bhaṭṭa Tauta
summary: The lost work on poetics and drama of Abhinavagupta's teacher Bhaṭṭa Tauta, known from Abhinava's citations; it is credited with the view that the experience of the hero, the poet and the spectator is the same.

title: Kāvyālaṅkāra of Bhāmaha
summary: The earliest surviving independent work on poetics after Bharata: poetry is word and meaning together (1.16); figures of speech rest on 'crooked' expression (vakrokti); it also criticizes grammarians' and logicians' positions.

structure.description: 6 paricchedas, c. 400 verses

title: Kāvyālaṅkāra of Rudraṭa
summary: Rudraṭa's treatise in sixteen chapters on figures, faults and rasa; it counts ten rasas, adding śānta and preyas ('affection') to Bharata's eight. Commented on by the Jain Namisādhu (1069).

structure.description: 16 adhyāyas

notes: The chapter giving the ten rasas is not fixed here.

title: Kāvyālaṅkāra-sāra-saṅgraha of Udbhaṭa
summary: Udbhaṭa's classification of figures of speech; the first to bring rasa into the figure called rasavat with the language of vibhāva and sthāyin.

title: Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra(vṛtti) of Vāmana
summary: Vāmana's aphorisms with his commentary: style (rīti) is the soul of poetry (1.2.6), style being a special arrangement of words made of qualities (guṇa).

structure.description: 5 adhikaraṇas

title: Kāvyamīmāṃsā of Rājaśekhara
summary: Rājaśekhara's 'inquiry into poetry', of which only the first of eighteen planned books survives: the myth of the Poetry-Man (kāvyapuruṣa) born of Sarasvatī, the kinds of poetic genius (pratibhā) — creative (kārayitrī) and appreciative (bhāvayitrī) — and the poet's training and daily routine.

title: Kāvyānuśāsana of Hemacandra
summary: Hemacandra's Jain manual of poetics with his own commentaries (Alaṅkāracūḍāmaṇi, Viveka), largely following Mammaṭa and Abhinavagupta on rasa.

title: Kāvyaprakāśa of Mammaṭa
summary: Mammaṭa's synthesis of poetics in ten chapters: the purposes and causes of poetry (1.2–3), its definition as faultless word and meaning with qualities (1.4), the three powers of words (denotation, indication, suggestion), rasa and bhāva (ch. 4) — love toward a deity is a bhāva, not a rasa — and śānta as the ninth rasa with dispassion as its stable emotion; the most commented work of the tradition.

title: Lalitā Sahasranāma
summary: The thousand names of Lalitā Mahātripurasundarī, framed as Hayagrīva's teaching to Agastya. The names describe her form and weapons, her city and palace, her war on Bhaṇḍāsura, her subtle body as the three sections of the Śrīvidyā mantra, her ascent as kuṇḍalinī through the cakras and knots, her qualityless nature, the three states and the fourth, the five cosmic acts, the Śrīcakra and her oneness with Śiva. Recitation and worship with the names are central Śākta practices.
location_in_parent: said to be in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, in the Hayagrīva-Agastya dialogue (colophon)

attribution.scholarly: Not part of the main printed Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa; a Śrīvidyā composition of uncertain date, authoritative by the time of Bhāskararāya (18th c.).

structure.description: An introductory part (pūrvabhāga, 51 verses in Bhāskararāya's count), the thousand names in 182½ anuṣṭubh verses with no name repeated and no filler particles, and a concluding part (phalaśruti); 320 verses in all by Bhāskararāya's count. The stotra proper is usually numbered 1-183.

attribution.scholarly: A composite work of many hands grown over several centuries around a narrative core; the frame narratives and the didactic books (esp. Śānti and Anuśāsana) are generally held to be later layers.

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa at the close of the Dvāpara yuga, before the Kali yuga (traditionally reckoned from 3102 BCE)

structure.description: 18 books (parvans), traditionally 100 sub-books (upaparvans) as listed in the Parvasaṃgraha (1.2); the Harivaṃśa is its supplement (khila). The tradition speaks of 100,000 verses (śatasāhasrī saṃhitā); 1.1.61 says Vyāsa made a 24,000-verse Bhārata without the sub-stories (upākhyānas); 1.1.50 records three starting points used by reciters (Manu, Āstīka, Uparicara). The critical text as digitized locally has 2,097 chapters and about 73,800 verse units.

summary: The great epic of the Bhārata war between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas, calling itself a 'fifth Veda' (kārṣṇa veda) and a treatise on dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa; besides the narrative it contains extended teaching sections (the Bhagavad Gītā, the Rājadharma, Āpaddharma and Mokṣadharma of the Śāntiparvan, the Anugītā, the Sanatsujātīya, Vidura's counsel, the Yakṣa's questions, the Nārāyaṇīya). It says of itself that what is found here on the four aims of life is found elsewhere, and what is not here is nowhere (1.56.33).

Its introduction (Paspaśā) asks what a word is, gives the purposes of studying grammar — protection of the Veda, adaptation of mantras, the scriptural command, brevity and certainty — tells how Bṛhaspati taught Indra words one by one for a thousand divine years without reaching the end, reads the Ṛgveda's 'four horns' verse as a praise of grammar, and holds that the Asuras were defeated for mispronouncing speech.

title: Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa

attribution.tradition: Mārkaṇḍeya tells Jaimini to go to the four wise birds (sons of Droṇa) in the Vindhya, who answer his questions (MkP 1-3; Matsya 53.25-26).
attribution.scholarly: One of the older Purāṇas, with little sectarian colouring; the Devī Māhātmya (chs. 81-93 in the Venkateshwara/Sansknet numbering, 78-90 in some others) is a separable later insertion.

tradition.text: Vyāsa, end of Dvāpara

scholarly.text: core c. 3rd-6th c. CE; Devī Māhātmya c. 5th-6th c. CE

structure.description: c. 134-137 chapters in full editions (the GRETIL/Sansknet e-text has chs. 1-93); 9,000 verses by the traditional count

notes: Chs. 10-15: Sumati ('Jaḍa') on death, the road of Yama and the hells, and Vipaścit; 16-44: Dattātreya's birth and his teaching (through Madālasā's son Alarka) - yoga chs. 39-43; 45-80: creation, time, cosmography and the manvantaras; 81-93: Devī Māhātmya. verse number checked in the GRETIL/Sansknet e-text of the MkP (chs. 1-93; Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81-93 in this numbering)
summary: A Purāṇa of dialogues: the birth, death and after-death journey of beings; the hells; Madālasā's teaching to her sons; Dattātreya's yoga for Alarka (posture, breath, dhāraṇā, obstacles, powers, Oṃ, the signs of death); creation, time and the fourteen manvantaras; and the Devī Māhātmya.

title: Mārkaṇḍeyasamāsyā (Mārkaṇḍeya's discourses)

tradition.text: composed by Vyāsa at the close of the Dvāpara yuga, before the Kali yuga (traditionally reckoned from 3102 BCE)

scholarly.text: composed and expanded in stages, c. 4th c. BCE – 4th c. CE

summary: The long-lived sage Mārkaṇḍeya instructs the exiled Pāṇḍavas: on karma, on the ages of the world and the dissolution — including his vision in the cosmic waters of a child on a banyan branch in whose body he saw the worlds — on the devoted wife and the righteous meat-seller, and other stories.

title: Maṭhāmnāya Upaniṣad
summary: A late text styled as an Upaniṣad describing the four monastic seats (āmnāya/maṭha) of the Daśanāmī order with their directions, sampradāyas, names, deities, Vedas and great sayings (e.g. western: Dvārakā, Sāmaveda, 'tat tvam asi'; eastern: Govardhana at Purī, Ṛgveda, 'prajñānaṃ brahma').

summary: A vṛtti on the SK that opens with the story of Kapila — an avatāra of the primal Person, son of Kardama and Devahūti — testing the brahmin Āsuri at thousand-year intervals before accepting him; it traces the teaching from Pañcaśikha through Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta and Devala to Īśvarakṛṣṇa, and enumerates the sixty topics of the Ṣaṣṭitantra.

attribution.scholarly: Among the older Purāṇas, with borrowings from the Vāyu; contains the standard descriptions of the eighteen Purāṇas.

tradition.text: Vyāsa, end of Dvāpara

scholarly.text: core c. 3rd-6th c. CE with later additions

structure.description: c. 290 chapters; 14,000 verses by the traditional count

notes: 53: definitions and gift-rules of the eighteen Purāṇas and some Upapurāṇas, the five marks, and the sāttvika/rājasa/tāmasa/saṅkīrṇa classification; later chapters: the sixteen great gifts (mahādāna), iconography (pratimā-lakṣaṇa), Prayāga and Avimukta (Vārāṇasī) māhātmyas. verse number checked in the local e-text of the Matsya Purāṇa (raw_etexts mAdhva-app)
summary: The Fish avatāra's teaching to Manu: creation, manvantaras, genealogies, vows and gifts (the sixteen great gifts), śrāddha, iconography and temple lore, tīrthas, and the authoritative descriptions of all the Purāṇas.

notes: Recalled: a partial critical edition exists (C. Kiss, Oxford DPhil); chapter count and contents to be checked in sourcing. Not available locally.

summary: A one-act farce set in Kāñcī. The drunken Kāpālika Satyasoma and his companion Devasomā lose their skull begging-bowl, accuse the Buddhist monk Nāgasena, appeal to the Pāśupata Babhrukalpa, and recover the bowl from a madman who took it from a dog. It satirises Kāpālika, Buddhist and Pāśupata ascetics.

summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); the fourth of the ten short treatises (daśa-prakaraṇa); it a short refutation of the doctrine of māyā (Advaita): if the self is self-luminous and without attributes, nothing in it is unknown for ignorance to cover, so the ignorance on which the doctrine rests is impossible.

summary: Jaimini's aphorisms on dharma known from Vedic injunction, in twelve adhyāyas (sixty pādas): (1) means of knowing dharma, (2) distinction of rites, (3) subsidiarity, (4) what prompts performance, (5) sequence, (6) eligibility, (7–8) general and specific transfer, (9) modification, (10) cancellation, (11) single performance for several, (12) incidental benefit. Its first pāda (the tarkapāda) grounds the authority of the authorless, eternal Veda.

title: Mugdhabodha
summary: Bopadeva's short non-Pāṇinian grammar, much used in Bengal.

title: Muhūrtacintāmaṇi
summary: Rāma Daivajña's standard manual of electional timing in 13 sections: good and bad times (tithis, weekdays, their lords and classes); the asterisms and their classes; solar ingresses; transits; the sacraments (saṃskāra); marriage with the eightfold matching; the bride's entry; the second coming; establishing the fires; royal consecration; journeys; building; and entering a house.

structure.description: 13 prakaraṇas

notes: Author's own commentary Pramitākṣarā; Govinda's Pīyūṣadhārā (1603).

title: Muhūrtamārtaṇḍa
summary: Nārāyaṇa's manual of electional astrology.

title: Mūka Pañcaśatī
summary: Five hundred verses to Kāmākṣī of Kāñcī in five centuries (on her āryā form, her lotus feet, praise, her glance and her smile), by the poet Mūka, who by tradition was mute until the Goddess's grace gave him speech.

structure.description: five śatakas: Āryā, Pādāravinda, Stuti, Kaṭākṣa, Mandasmita

title: Mukhabimbāgama

attribution.tradition: revealed by Sadāśiva from the upper (Īśāna) face; first received by Praśānta, then Dadhīci (Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92; Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10)
attribution.scholarly: texts now transmitted under this title are mostly South Indian redactions centred on temple ritual; their relation to the early scripture of the same name is not established here

structure.description: Rudrabheda no. 20 in the Kāmika's order; 15 upabhedas in the Kāmika's list

notes: Kiraṇa 10.15/10.21: Praśānta → the sage Dadhīca. Śrīkaṇṭhīya: 'Mukhabimba'. In the Kāmika's image of the scriptures as Sadāśiva's body it is the face (pūrva 1.93–101). Lists checked by the Phase-B author against local e-texts: Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/Kamikagama.md (Kāmika Pūrvabhāga, Madras 1909 Grantha ed. as transcribed)), Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10.3–27 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/kiranagama.md (Kiraṇa vidyāpāda, South Indian printed text as transcribed)) and the Śrīkaṇṭhīya list quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)).
summary: No. 20 of the 28 Śaiva Siddhānta mūlāgamas (Rudrabheda). According to the Kāmika it was first received by Praśānta, then Dadhīci. The Kāmika assigns it 15 upabheda(s): Caturmukha, Alāyoga (reading uncertain), Saṃstobha, Pratibimbaka, Ātmālaṅkāra, Vāyavya, Tauṭika, Tuṭinīraka, Kalātyaya, Tulāyoga, Kuṭṭima, Paṭṭaśekhara, Mahāvidyā, Mahāsaura, Bimba.

title: Muktāphala
summary: Vopadeva's anthology of Bhāgavata verses arranged under the themes of devotion (the Lord, his avatāras, the forms and fruits of devotion, and the devotional rasas), with the commentary Kaivalyadīpikā by Hemādri.
notes: The arrangement by nine devotional rasas is recalled with low confidence.

title: Vacanas of Muktāyakka
summary: Vacanas of the woman śaraṇa who, grieving her brother Ajagaṇṇa, questioned Allama and was questioned by him; they treat grief, speech and silence, and realization.
notes: Cited by incipit; edition numbering to be fixed in Phase D.

title: Muktikā Upaniṣad

attribution.scholarly: anonymous; assigned to a Veda by the Muktikā list, not by any surviving śākhā transmission

tradition.text: Śruti; Rāma's teaching to Hanumān in the Tretā age (narrative frame)

scholarly.text: Late: presupposes the sectarian and Yoga/Sannyāsa collections; generally put in the later medieval period (exact date unknown); the list reflects a South Indian Advaita canon

summary: Rāma teaches Hanumān the canon of 108 Upaniṣads with their Vedas, the kinds of liberation, graded study for liberation and the rules of eligibility; ch.2 teaches liberation while living through the joint practice of destroying vāsanā, dissolving mind and knowing the truth.

editions.name: Īśādiviṃśottaraśatopaniṣadaḥ (Nirṇayasāgara collection of 120 Upaniṣads), South Indian recension carrying Upaniṣad Brahmayogin's opening maṅgala verses; e-text github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts vedaH/misc/upaniShat/mixedPF/108_Upanishads.md

key_teachings_note: 17 skeleton teachings in this shard; first 8 listed

title: Muktivāda (Raghudeva)
summary: A Navya-Nyāya treatise on liberation that opens with the Ācārya's (Udayana's) definition of liberation as the absolute cessation of pain and refines 'absolute' in technical terms; one of a set of vāda texts attributed to Raghudeva Bhaṭṭācārya.

editions.name: Navyanyāyavādagranthāḥ (Delhi Sanskrit Academy 2008), sanskrit/raw_etexts (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts) nyAya-shAstram/navyanyAya-vAda-granthaH

notes: Attribution follows the local e-text header; the same collection contains Īśvaravāda, Prāgabhāvavāda, Ākāṅkṣāvāda, Sāmagrīvāda and other vādas.

title: Mukundamālā
summary: Sanskrit hymn to Mukunda (Kṛṣṇa) attributed to Kulaśekhara: the devotee asks not for dharma, wealth or pleasure but only for unwavering devotion to the Lord's feet in every birth, and asks that the mind enter the Lord's feet now, since at death, with the throat choked, remembrance may fail.

attribution.tradition: Composed by Kulaśekhara Āḻvār, the king-devotee of Kerala.
attribution.scholarly: Commonly accepted as by a Kulaśekhara of Kerala; the identification with the Āḻvār and with the author of the Sanskrit dramas Tapatīsaṃvaraṇa and Subhadrādhanañjaya is debated.

scholarly.text: c. 9th c. CE if by the Āḻvār

structure.description: c. 34–40 verses; recensions differ in number and order

notes: Verse numbers differ between recensions; teachings are therefore cited by incipit.

title: Mūlāvidyānirāsa
summary: Swami Satchidanandendra Sarasvati's (recent) Sanskrit polemic arguing that Śaṅkara did not teach a positive root-ignorance (mūlāvidyā) and that the Vivaraṇa and later schools depart from him.

title: Mumukṣuppaṭi
summary: Piḷḷai Lokācārya's aphoristic Maṇipravāḷa work for 'one seeking liberation' on the three secret mantras — the tirumantra, the dvaya and the carama-śloka — in three sections.

tradition.text: Piḷḷai Lokācārya, 1205–1311 CE in commonly given Teṅkalai dates

title: Mumukṣuppaṭi-vyākhyānam
summary: Maṇavāḷa Māmuni's commentary on the Mumukṣuppaṭi.

tradition.text: Maṇavāḷa Māmuni, 1370–1443 CE (traditional)

title: Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad

attribution.tradition: śruti, 'seen' by the sages whose teaching it records; not a human composition
attribution.scholarly: anonymous compilation within the Vedic schools (śākhās), incorporating older materials

tradition.text: Revealed scripture (śruti): in the Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta view without human author and beginningless; the texts themselves trace their teaching through lineages of teachers back to Brahma/Prajāpati and brahman, the self-existent

structure.description: 3 mundakas of 2 khandas each, in verse (65 verses in Śaṅkara's text; 64 where 2.2.7 is one verse)

summary: Aṅgiras teaches Śaunaka the higher knowledge by which the imperishable is grasped, above the lower knowledge of the Vedas and their limbs; sacrifices are unsafe boats; one must go to a teacher fuel in hand; all comes from the imperishable like sparks from fire; Om is the bow, the self the arrow, brahman the target; the two birds on one tree; truth alone conquers; renunciants purified by saṃnyāsa-yoga are released.

editions.name: Sanskrit text with Śaṅkara's bhasya (Advaita-Sarada e-text; GitHub sanskrit/raw_etexts mirror)
editions.licence: public domain text; e-text licence per repository

editions.name: R. E. Hume, The Thirteen Principal Upanishads (1921)
F. Max Muller, The Upanishads, SBE 1 and 15 (1879, 1884)

notes: Veda affiliation: Atharvaveda (traditionally the Śaunaka śākhā)

title: Ātharvaṇopaniṣad-bhāṣya (Madhva)

attribution.tradition: Madhva (Ānandatīrtha), counted among his thirty-seven works
attribution.scholarly: accepted as Madhva's

tradition.text: composed by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha); the tradition dates his life to 1199–1278 or 1238–1317

summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); Madhva's commentary on the Ātharvaṇa (Muṇḍaka) Upaniṣad, reading it as teaching Viṣṇu's supremacy and his difference from souls and matter, often by etymological explanation of names and by quotations from other scriptures.

title: Muṇḍakopaniṣadbhāṣya of Śaṅkara
summary: Śaṅkara's commentary distinguishing the lower (aparā) and higher (parā) knowledge and insisting on approaching a teacher learned in scripture and established in Brahman (1.2.12).

title: Muṇḍamālā Tantra
summary: An eastern tantra that names the ten Mahāvidyās — Kālī, Tārā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, Dhūmāvatī, Bagalā, Mātaṅgī and Kamalā — as 'siddha-vidyās' needing no preliminary tests (as quoted in Kṛṣṇānanda's Tantrasāra), and treats their worship, rosaries and mantras.

editions.name: Muktabodha Digital Library e-text M00537-M00538

title: Munivāhanabhoga
summary: Vedānta Deśika's commentary on Tiruppāṇ Āḻvār's Amalaṉātipirāṉ (the Āḻvār 'carried by the sage', munivāhana), reading its ten verses as containing the essence of Vedānta.

title: Mūṉṟām Tiruvantāti
summary: Pēyāḻvār's hundred veṇpās, the 'third' antāti, opening with the vision in the lamplight: 'I have seen Śrī, I have seen the golden form ...'.

structure.description: 100 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

tradition.text: close of the Dvāpara age (hagiographies)

title: Mūrti Rahasya
summary: The third 'secret': the forms of the Goddess foretold in the Devī Māhātmya's eleventh chapter (Nandā, Raktadantikā, Śākambharī, Durgā, Bhīmā, Bhrāmarī) and their meditation.
notes: Recited as a limb (aṅga) of the Durgā Saptaśatī (Devī Māhātmya, U07); U23 records the Śākta liturgy.

title: Mutal Tiruvantāti
summary: Poykai Āḻvār's hundred veṇpās, the 'first' antāti, sung (in the tradition's account) in the dark vestibule at Tirukkōvalūr: it opens by lighting a lamp with the earth as bowl, the sea as ghee and the sun as flame.

structure.description: 100 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

tradition.text: close of the Dvāpara age (hagiographies)

title: Naam or Word

attribution.tradition: by Kirpal Singh

summary: Kirpal Singh's comparative exposition of the Word (Nām, śabd, logos, kalma) as the power that creates and sustains, heard within as sound and seen as light.

title: Nācciyār Tirumoḻi
summary: Āṇṭāḷ's 143 verses in 14 decads: prayer to Kāma to unite her with Kṛṣṇa, the dream of her wedding ('vāraṇam āyiram'), questions to the conch about the taste of his lips, messages to clouds and birds, the agony of separation, and at the end the sight of him in Vṛndāvana.

structure.description: 143 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

tradition.text: early Kali age (hagiographies)

title: Nādabindu Upaniṣad

canon.group_scheme: editorial grouping of the 108 used by the Adyar Library series and most modern catalogues; the Muktikā itself lists the 108 by Veda only

attribution.tradition: Śruti: revealed, without human author (apauruṣeya); the Muktikā presents it as one of the 108 Upaniṣads that Rāma teaches Hanumān, each belonging to a Vedic śākhā
attribution.scholarly: anonymous; assigned to a Veda by the Muktikā list, not by any surviving śākhā transmission

tradition.text: Śruti: eternal and authorless; no human date

scholarly.text: Scholarly accounts differ by text. Several Yoga Upaniṣads (e.g. Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kṣurikā, Tejobindu, Nādabindu, Dhyānabindu, Brahmavidyā, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā, Haṃsa) survive in shorter northern versions that are older; the expanded southern recensions (as in this collection) borrow from medieval haṭha works and were probably compiled in South India, perhaps as late as the 18th c. (Bouy 1994).

summary: Oṃ as a bird; the twelve measures and the destinies of one who dies in each; prārabdha for the knower; siddhāsana, vaiṣṇavī mudrā and listening within the right ear; inner sounds in early, middle and late stages; mind absorbed in nāda like milk in water; the soundless as Brahman and the state of unmanī.

title: Nādakārikā
summary: A short verse treatise on nāda (sound) and the nature of mantras and speech in the Siddhānta, attributed to Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, with Aghoraśiva's commentary.

attribution.tradition: Rāmakaṇṭha
attribution.scholarly: usually taken as Rāmakaṇṭha II; low confidence

title: Nādānusandhāna

attribution.tradition: Spoken by Śiva to the Goddess.

structure.description: a short tract of a few dozen verses (not counted precisely)

summary: A short dialogue in which Śiva teaches the unstruck inner sound in ten forms (ciṇī, ciñciṇī, ciri, conch, strings, a ringing, bronze cymbals, cloud, roaring water, kettle-drum) — the first nine to be left and the tenth giving liberation — and correlates the sounds with the elements and their maṇḍalas and with the dissolution of the principles.

editions.name: Muktabodha e-text M00526 (from NGMCP A62/11)
eBhāratī-Sampat e-text Ebharati-11931

notes: Distinct from the Nādabindu Upaniṣad and from the nāda chapter of the Haṭhapradīpikā. Date and provenance unknown to this unit. The e-texts are corrupt in places.

title: Nāḍī granthas (palm-leaf nāḍīs)
summary: The corpus of palm-leaf 'nāḍī' readings — Agastya, Kauśika, Bhṛgu, Śiva and other nāḍīs — which the tradition holds were written by the seers for each future consultant, organized by thumb-impression classes and chapters (kāṇḍa) on life, past births and remedies.

attribution.tradition: written by ancient seers
attribution.scholarly: manuscripts and practice largely recent and unedited

title: Nāḍīparīkṣā
summary: A short late treatise on pulse examination, attributed in its colophons to Kaṇāda.

title: Naiṣkarmyasiddhi

structure.description: 4 chapters

summary: Sureśvara's treatise (verse with prose) establishing 'actionlessness': ch. 1 refutes the view that works, alone or combined with knowledge, lead to liberation; ch. 2 separates the self from the not-self by agreement and difference; ch. 3 explains how 'tat tvam asi' gives immediate knowledge; ch. 4 summarizes and describes the knower, whose virtues arise without effort and who cannot act licentiously.

title: Nālāyira Divya Prabandham
summary: The 'four thousand divine compositions': the collected hymns of the twelve Āḻvārs (with Tiruvaraṅkattu Amutaṉār's Irāmāṉuca Nūṟṟantāti), gathered and arranged by Nāthamuni, set to music for temple recitation, and revered by Śrīvaiṣṇavas as the Tamil Veda. It sings Tirumāl with Śrī in his temple images, the avatāras, surrender, service, the name, and love in the voices of Tamil love-poetry.

attribution.tradition: Sung by the twelve Āḻvārs; lost and recovered by Nāthamuni, who received all four thousand from Nammāḻvār in yogic vision at Kurukūr after reciting Madhurakavi's Kaṇṇinuṇ Ciṟuttāmpu 12,000 times.
attribution.scholarly: Compiled c. 10th c. CE from hymns composed c. 6th–9th c.; the four-part arrangement and the inclusion of the Irāmāṉuca Nūṟṟantāti reflect later Śrīvaiṣṇava redaction.

tradition.text: hymns of the late Dvāpara and early Kali ages, recovered by Nāthamuni

scholarly.text: hymns c. 6th–9th c. CE; compiled c. 10th c. CE

structure.description: About 4000 verses in four 'thousands' (āyiram): (1) Mutalāyiram (c. 947: Tiruppallāṇṭu, Periyāḻvār Tirumoḻi, Tiruppāvai, Nācciyār Tirumoḻi, Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi, Tiruccanta Viruttam, Tirumālai, Tiruppaḷḷiyeḻucci, Amalaṉātipirāṉ, Kaṇṇinuṇ Ciṟuttāmpu); (2) Periya Tirumoḻi with Tirukkuṟuntāṇṭakam and Tiruneṭuntāṇṭakam (c. 1134); (3) Iyaṟpā, the recited portion (c. 817: the first three Tiruvantātis, Nāṉmukaṉ Tiruvantāti, Tiruviruttam, Tiruvāciriyam, Periya Tiruvantāti, Tiruveḻukkūṟṟirukkai, Ciṟiya and Periya Tirumaṭal, Irāmāṉuca Nūṟṟantāti); (4) Tiruvāymoḻi (1102). Each work is preceded by invocatory taṉiyaṉ verses.

notes: Part counts (947 / 1134 / 817 / 1102 = 4000) as recalled, counting Ciṟiya Tirumaṭal as 40 and Periya Tirumaṭal as 78 units; placement of Tirukkuṟuntāṇṭakam/Tiruneṭuntāṇṭakam differs in some arrangements. Commentaries: see src:tiruvaymoli and the U14 commentary entries (src:arayirappati etc.). Periyavāccāṉ Piḷḷai commented on nearly the whole Prabandham.

title: Nām-ghoṣā (Hājārī-ghoṣā)
summary: Mādhavadeva's thousand verses on the name and on devotion: bowing first to the devotees who do not desire even liberation, it teaches the name of Kṛṣṇa, service to the guru and the company of devotees as the whole path.

attribution.tradition: Mādhavadeva's.
attribution.scholarly: Accepted.

structure.description: about 1,000 verses

title: Nāmdev Gāthā
summary: The Marathi abhaṅgas ascribed to Nāmdev (some 2,500) — childhood intimacy with Viṭṭhala, the name and kīrtan, the saints of his circle, the Tīrthāvaḷī (pilgrimage with Jñāneśvar) and the Samādhi songs on Jñāneśvar's entering samādhi — together with his Hindi padas, some of which are preserved in the Sikh scripture (context only).

attribution.tradition: Nāmdev's; he vowed to compose a hundred crore abhaṅgas and his household (Janābāī) completed them.
attribution.scholarly: A large corpus with layers; several later Nāmdevs (e.g. Viṣṇudās Nāmā) may be mixed in.

tradition.text: Nāmdev 1270–1350

title: Nandī Sūtra
summary: A Cūlikāsūtra (a Mūlasūtra for Sthānakavāsīs): opening hymns to Mahāvīra, the saṅgha and the line of elders, then a treatise on the five kinds of knowledge (mati, śruta, avadhi, manaḥparyaya, kevala), with the classification of scripture (aṅga-praviṣṭa and aṅga-bāhya, kālika and utkālika), the contents of the twelve Aṅgas, and the teaching that the twelve-limbed canon is eternal.

title: Nandikeśvara-kāśikā
summary: U31 contribution: the verse commentary reading the fourteen Māheśvara sūtras (the phoneme list sounded by Śiva's drum) as teachings on the supreme and its manifestation — the letter a as the supreme Lord and the sounds as the unfolding of Śiva and Śakti; a bridge between grammar and mantra theory.
alt_summary: A short verse commentary ascribed to Nandikeśvara that reads the fourteen Māheśvara sūtras as teachings on the supreme reality and its manifestation; it opens with the story that at the end of his dance Śiva, the king of dancers, sounded his drum fourteen times to uplift Sanaka and the other perfected sages.
notes: Date and verse numbers not verified; the opening story is widely quoted.

title: Nāṉmukaṉ Tiruvantāti
summary: Tirumaḻicai Āḻvār's 96 veṇpās, opening 'Nārāyaṇa created the four-faced one' — a sustained assertion of Nārāyaṇa's supremacy over Brahmā and Śiva and of refuge in him alone.

structure.description: 96 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

tradition.text: close of the Dvāpara age (hagiographies)

title: Nañvāda
summary: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi's treatise on the meaning of the negative particle (nañ).

title: Nārada Bhakti Sūtra
summary: Eighty-four aphorisms attributed to the sage Nārada defining devotion as supreme love (parama-prema) of the nature of nectar, 'the fruit itself', higher than action, knowledge and yoga; they give earlier teachers' definitions and the gopīs as the model, the means (renunciation, unceasing worship, hearing and singing, above all the grace of great souls), the things to avoid, the signs of the lover of God, the eleven forms of attachment, and the line of bhakti teachers.

attribution.tradition: Spoken by the divine sage Nārada ('nārada-proktam', NBS 84).
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous; usually dated after the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, c. 10th–13th c. CE or later.

scholarly.text: c. 10th–13th c. CE or later (no consensus)

structure.description: 84 sūtras (numbering varies slightly between editions); sometimes divided into five chapters (adhyāyas) in modern editions

notes: Sūtra numbering follows the common 84-sūtra text; some editions divide or join sūtras differently, so numbers may shift by one or two. No pre-modern Sanskrit commentary recalled with confidence; modern commentaries are many (e.g. in the Ramakrishna and ISKCON movements) and are not recorded here.

title: Nārada Purāṇa
alt_titles: Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa (so named in the printed colophons)

attribution.tradition: Nārada's teaching of the dharmas of the Bṛhat-kalpa (Matsya 53.23); the four Kumāras (Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatkumāra, Sanātana) instruct Nārada.
attribution.scholarly: The Mahāpurāṇa is distinguished by scholars from a separate Bṛhannāradīya Upapurāṇa, but printed colophons of the Mahāpurāṇa use 'Bṛhannāradīya'.

tradition.text: Vyāsa, end of Dvāpara

alt_summary: The Śikṣā of the Sāmaveda: it relates the Vedic accents and the tones of sāman chanting to the seven musical notes (svara) beginning with ṣaḍja, and treats the grāmas, mūrchanās and the manner of singing — a bridge between Vedic phonetics and the later science of music.
