title: Nyāyāmṛta

structure.description: 4 paricchedas

summary: Vyāsatīrtha's great polemic against Advaita, in four chapters that follow the four chapters of the Brahmasūtras: (1) the reality of the world — a refutation of the five Advaita definitions of falsity (mithyātva) and of the inferences from perceivability, insentience and limitedness; (2) the Upaniṣads do not teach an impartite, attributeless meaning, and the flawless Brahman is absolutely different from the flawed souls; (3) the means — against the Vivaraṇa view of hearing, reflection and meditation, the Lord is to be won by direct realization born of meditation; (4) liberation is not the mere cessation of ignorance, and the liberated, from Brahmā and Rudra down, are graded. Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi answers it point by point.
notes: Four paricchedas, their opening sections and concluding sentences checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions.

title: Nyāyāmṛta-āmoda (Laghvāmoda)
summary: Vijayīndra Tīrtha's commentary on Vyāsatīrtha's Nyāyāmṛta.
notes: A 'Laghvāmoda' commentary on the Nyāyāmṛta is in the raw_etexts corpus; its attribution to Vijayīndra is inferred from the file name ('vijayayati') and memory.

title: Nyāyāmṛta-taraṅgiṇī
summary: Vyāsa Rāmācārya's commentary on the Nyāyāmṛta, defending it against Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi; Brahmānanda Sarasvatī's Laghucandrikā replies to it.

title: Nyāyamuktāvalī (Rāghavendra)

tradition.text: Rāghavendra entered his brindāvana at Mantrālaya in 1671

summary: Rāghavendra Tīrtha's concise commentary on the Brahmasūtras in Madhva's reading, stating the conclusion of each adhikaraṇa (e.g., that liberation is the principal fruit of knowledge).
notes: Author checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions.

title: Nyāyanirṇaya
summary: Ānandagiri's gloss on Śaṅkara's BSBh; Ānandagiri also glossed Śaṅkara's Upaniṣad and Gītā commentaries.

title: Nyāyapariśuddhi
summary: Deśika's 'purification of Nyāya': Viśiṣṭādvaita logic and epistemology (perception, inference, scripture, and the theory of error), following Nāthamuni's lost Nyāyatattva and correcting Nyāya where it conflicts with Vedānta.

tradition.text: Vedānta Deśika, 1268–1369 CE (traditional)

title: Nyāyarakṣāmaṇi
summary: Appayya Dīkṣita's Advaita commentary on the adhikaraṇas of the first pāda(s) of the Brahma Sūtras.

title: Nyāyaratna
summary: Maṇikaṇṭha Miśra's pre-Gaṅgeśa work on inference and related topics, regarded as a forerunner of Navya-Nyāya.
notes: Low confidence on title details; listed as a gap to check.

title: Nyāyaratnākara

editions.name: with the Ślokavārttika, ebhāratī-sampat digital text

summary: Pārthasārathi Miśra's commentary on the Ślokavārttika; it names Bhartṛmitra among those who had made Mīmāṃsā 'Lokāyata'.

title: Nyāyaratnamālā
summary: Pārthasārathi Miśra's independent treatise on selected Mīmāṃsā topics (e.g. the validity of cognition, injunction).

title: Nyāyaratnāvalī (Padmanābha Tīrtha)
summary: Padmanābha Tīrtha's commentary on the Anuvyākhyāna, preceding Jayatīrtha's Nyāyasudhā.
notes: Disambiguated from Brahmānanda Sarasvatī's Advaita Nyāyaratnāvalī (on the Siddhāntabindu). Title recalled, not verified.

title: Nyāyasāra

structure.description: 3 paricchedas (pratyakṣa, anumāna, āgama)

summary: Bhāsarvajña's manual in three chapters (perception, inference, verbal testimony): it accepts only three means of knowledge, treats yogic perception, and holds — against the mainstream — that liberation is the absolute cessation of pain together with the experience of eternal bliss; its last part links the path to Śaiva yoga.

title: Nyāyasiddhāñjana
summary: Deśika's treatise on the categories of Viśiṣṭādvaita — insentient substance, soul, Lord, the eternal realm, cognition and non-substances.

tradition.text: Vedānta Deśika, 1268–1369 CE (traditional)

title: Nyāyasiddhāntadīpa
summary: Śaśadhara's pre-Gaṅgeśa treatise on Nyāya topics.

title: Nyāyasiddhāntamuktāvalī

scholarly.text: first half of the 17th c. CE

summary: Viśvanātha's auto-commentary on the Bhāṣāpariccheda, the standard intermediate text of syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika in Navya-Nyāya idiom (e.g. its inference of a maker from the effecthood of earth, sprouts and the like).

editions.name: sanskrit/raw_etexts (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts) nyAya-shAstram/nyAya_siddhAnta_muktAvaliH_2_Tika.pdf.txt.md (OCR, with Dinakarī and Rāmarudrī)

title: Nyāyasūcīnibandha

scholarly.text: 841 CE (if Vikrama era) or 976 CE (if Śaka era)

summary: Vācaspati Miśra's index of the sūtras and prakaraṇas of the Nyāya Sūtra, which fixed the sūtra text as read by the later tradition; its closing verse gives a date (year 898 of an unnamed era).

title: Nyāyasudhā
summary: Jayatīrtha's great commentary on Madhva's Anuvyākhyāna, the most authoritative exposition of Dvaita doctrine and polemic, esteemed in the tradition as its central scholastic text; it expands Madhva's arguments against Advaita, Buddhist, Jain, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā and Sāṃkhya positions.

title: Nyāyasudhā-parimala

tradition.text: Rāghavendra entered his brindāvana at Mantrālaya in 1671

summary: Rāghavendra Tīrtha's commentary on Jayatīrtha's Nyāyasudhā, from which he is called Parimalācārya.

title: Nyāyasudhā (Rāṇaka)
notes: Distinct from Jayatīrtha's Dvaita Nyāyasudhā (src:nyayasudha).
summary: Someśvara Bhaṭṭa's commentary on Kumārila's Tantravārttika, known as Rāṇaka.

title: Nyāyasūtravṛtti (Viśvanātha)

scholarly.text: 1634 CE (date given in the text, as usually reported)

summary: Viśvanātha Nyāyapañcānana's running commentary on the Nyāya Sūtra, in Navya-Nyāya idiom.

title: Nyāyatattva
summary: Nāthamuni's lost work on logic and the means of knowledge, which later Viśiṣṭādvaita logicians (Vedānta Deśika's Nyāyapariśuddhi) say they follow; known only from citations.

tradition.text: Nāthamuni, traditionally 9th–10th c. (hagiographies give an extremely long life)

title: Nyāyavivaraṇa

attribution.tradition: Madhva (Ānandatīrtha), counted among his thirty-seven works
attribution.scholarly: accepted as Madhva's

tradition.text: composed by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha); the tradition dates his life to 1199–1278 or 1238–1317

summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); a short prose work setting out, adhikaraṇa by adhikaraṇa, the reasoning (nyāya) by which Madhva reads the Brahmasūtras.

title: Oghaniryukti
summary: A text on the general (ogha) rules of monastic life — inspection, alms, equipment, lodging — counted as the fourth Mūlasūtra in some Mūrtipūjaka lists instead of or together with the Piṇḍaniryukti.

title: Oṉpatiṉāyirappaṭi (the 'Nine Thousand')
summary: Nañjīyar's Maṇipravāḷa commentary on the Tiruvāymoḻi; the tradition says the copy made by Nampiḷḷai was lost in the Kāvēri and rewritten by him from memory.

title: Oṣadhi Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.97)
summary: The physician's hymn to the healing plants, born three ages before the gods; where plants gather like kings in assembly, that inspired one is called a physician, slayer of demons and dispeller of disease.

attribution.tradition: seen by bhisag-atharvana; deity: the plants (oṣadhayaḥ) (Sarvānukramaṇī)
attribution.scholarly: a hymn of the Ṛgveda; books 1 and 10 are among its later layers

checks.note: Hymn located in the local Śākala text. 23 verses; seer Bhiṣag Ātharvaṇa.

title: Oupnek'hat
summary: Anquetil-Duperron's Latin rendering (1801–1802) of the Persian Sirr-i Akbar; the first Upaniṣad collection widely read in Europe.

title: Padacandrikā of Anantadeva
summary: A short word-by-word commentary on the sūtras by Anantadeva, who says he made this Padacandrikā after examining 'the vṛtti on the meaning of the sūtras' and offers it at the feet of Śiva (closing verse); it glosses nirodha as the mind's inward dissolution into its cause (1.2).
notes: Date not established (gap).

title: Padamañjarī
summary: Haradatta's sub-commentary on the Kāśikāvṛtti.
notes: Whether this Haradatta is the Dharmasūtra commentator of the same name is uncertain.

title: Padaratnāvalī
summary: Vijayadhvaja Tīrtha's word-by-word commentary on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the standard Mādhva commentary on it.

title: Padārthādarśa of Rāghavabhaṭṭa
summary: Rāghavabhaṭṭa's learned commentary on the Śāradātilaka, finished in Vārāṇasī in 1493/94, which quotes a very wide range of Āgamas, Tantras and Purāṇas; among them the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā's definitions of spoken, whispered and mental japa.
notes: Wording and locator checked in Phase B against a local e-text in sources_raw/; still a skeleton entry (not fidelity-checked).
alt_summary: Rāghavabhaṭṭa's commentary on the Śāradātilaka, rich in quotations from lost tantras.

title: Padārthadharmasaṅgraha
summary: Praśastapāda's systematic exposition of Vaiśeṣika (often called Praśastapādabhāṣya, though not a line-by-line commentary): after saluting Īśvara and Kaṇāda it declares knowledge of the similarities and dissimilarities of the six categories the cause of the highest good, arising from dharma manifested by the Lord's command; it fixes twenty-four qualities, gives the account of cosmic dissolution and creation by Maheśvara's will, divides cognition into knowledge (perception, inference, memory, seers' knowledge) and its opposites, treats yogic perception, dharma and adharma, and liberation.
notes: Commentaries: Vyomaśiva's Vyomavatī, Śrīdhara's Nyāyakandalī, Udayana's Kiraṇāvalī, and later ones.

title: Padārthatattvanirūpaṇa
summary: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi's critical re-examination of the Vaiśeṣika list of categories, proposing reductions and additions to the traditional seven.
notes: The specific revisions (e.g. treatment of space, time and ultimate particularity) are recalled with low confidence and are not asserted as teachings in this skeleton.

title: Padma Purāṇa

attribution.tradition: Compiled by Vyāsa (Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana) from the one primeval Purāṇa and taught through Romaharṣaṇa and his line. Told of the time when the world was a golden lotus (Matsya 53.14).
attribution.scholarly: Survives in two main recensions - a Bengal recension in five khaṇḍas and a South Indian/Ānandāśrama recension in six khaṇḍas (the Venkateshwara print arranges Sṛṣṭi, Bhūmi, Svarga, Brahma, Pātāla, Uttara and Kriyāyogasāra); many layers of different date.

tradition.text: Vyāsa, end of Dvāpara

structure.description: khaṇḍas differing by recension; 55,000 verses by the traditional count (BhP 12.13.4; Matsya 53.14)

notes: Contains the Bhāgavata-māhātmya (Uttarakhaṇḍa; colophon checked in the local e-text), the Gītā-māhātmya, the Śiva Gītā (U06), the classification of the Purāṇas by the three guṇas (Uttarakhaṇḍa; ch. number edition-dependent, often cited as 236.18-21), and the list of ten offences against the name as cited by Gauḍīya authors.
summary: A vast Vaiṣṇava-leaning compendium: creation, tīrthas (Puṣkara and others), vratas (Ekādaśī, Kārttika, Māgha), the glory of the Bhāgavata and the Gītā, Rāma narratives, the worship of the name and of the śālagrāma and tulasī, and the guṇa-classification of the eighteen Purāṇas.

title: Pādma Saṃhitā

attribution.tradition: revealed by Bhagavān (Nārāyaṇa/Vāsudeva); one of the traditional 108 saṃhitās

structure.description: jñānapāda, yogapāda, kriyāpāda, caryāpāda

editions.name: Pādma Saṃhitā, Pāñcarātra Pariśodhana Pariṣad, Madras (caryāpāda 1974; other pādas 1982)

notes: eBhāratī e-text consulted locally (padmasaMhitA.md).
summary: Pāñcarātra saṃhitā in the four pādas (jñāna, yoga, kriyā, caryā), presented as the expansion of the Jayākhya and followed in practice at Hastiśaila (Kāñcī). Its jñānapāda praises the Pāñcarātra above all śāstras, explains the name (other systems become 'night' before it) and divides it into four siddhāntas (1.60–83).

title: Padmāvat
summary: Malik Muhammad Jāyasī's Avadhi epic (1540), in which King Ratansen takes the yogī's guise — earrings, patched cloak, horn and begging bowl — to seek Padmāvatī; context for the Nāth insignia in the 16th century.
notes: Sufi-context literature, context only.

title: Pādukāpañcaka

attribution.tradition: spoken by Śiva
attribution.scholarly: anonymous; transmitted with the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa

scholarly.text: uncertain; before the 18th-c. commentary of Kālīcaraṇa

structure.description: 7 verses (with Kālīcaraṇa's commentary)

summary: 'The Five-fold Footstool': a hymn on the guru's sandals (pādukā) meditated upon in the thousand-petalled lotus — the white lotus, the triangle of the letters a-ka-tha, the haṃsa, the two sandals of light and the jewelled seat — as the culmination of the inner ascent.

editions.name: in Avalon, The Serpent Power (1919)

title: Pādukāsahasra
summary: Deśika's 1,008 verses in 32 sections (paddhati) on the sandals of Raṅganātha, composed, the tradition says, in a single night; the sandals are Nammāḻvār (Śaṭhakopa) and the teacher who carries the Lord to the devotee.

tradition.text: Vedānta Deśika, 1268–1369 CE (traditional)

title: Padyāvalī
summary: Rūpa's anthology of devotional verses by many poets, including the verses later gathered as Caitanya's Śikṣāṣṭaka.

title: Paiṅgala Upaniṣad

summary: After twelve years' service Paiṅgala asks Yājñavalkya: the emergence of the world from the witness and mūlaprakṛti, Īśvara, Hiraṇyagarbha and Virāṭ; quintuplication; the three bodies; the jīva's states; the great sayings; jīvanmukti and videhamukti.

title: Paitāmaha Siddhānta
summary: The siddhānta ascribed to Pitāmaha (Brahmā); its early form, close to the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, is summarized in the Pañcasiddhāntikā; a later form is preserved in the Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa and underlies Brahmagupta's work.
notes: Known chiefly through Varāhamihira's Pañcasiddhāntikā.

title: Pākhaṇḍ-khaṇḍinī (commentary on the Bījak)

attribution.tradition: by Mahārāj Viśvanāth Siṃh of Rewā
attribution.scholarly: 19th c.; reads Kabīr's Rām in a Rāma-bhakti sense

summary: A royal commentary on the Bījak, 'the destroyer of hypocrisy', which reads Kabīr's critique of outward religion within a Vaiṣṇava Rāma-bhakti frame.

title: Tipiṭaka (the Pali Canon)
summary: The three 'baskets' of the Theravāda canon — Vinaya (monastic discipline), Sutta (discourses) and Abhidhamma (analysis of phenomena) — held to be the word of the Buddha as rehearsed at the First Council and transmitted orally until written down in Sri Lanka.

structure.description: Vinaya Piṭaka (Suttavibhaṅga, Khandhaka, Parivāra); Sutta Piṭaka (Dīgha, Majjhima, Saṃyutta, Aṅguttara and Khuddaka Nikāyas); Abhidhamma Piṭaka (seven books: Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, Paṭṭhāna)

tradition.text: rehearsed at the First Council at Rājagaha in the first rains after the parinibbāna (543 BCE by the Theravāda reckoning); written down on palm leaves at the Āloka-vihāra (Aluvihāra), Sri Lanka, under King Vaṭṭagāmaṇī Abhaya

scholarly.text: oral composition and redaction c. 5th–1st c. BCE; first written c. 29–17 BCE (Vaṭṭagāmaṇī); later KN books and the Abhidhamma the latest strata

title: Paltū Sāhib kī Bānī

attribution.tradition: the verses of Paltū Sāhib of Ayodhyā
attribution.scholarly: Belvedere Press edition in three parts

summary: Paltū's forceful verses against hypocrisy and for the inner Name and sound; much used in Sant Mat literature.

title: Pāmpāṭṭic cittar pāṭalkaḷ (the songs of the snake-charmer Siddhar)
summary: Songs with the refrain 'āṭu pāmpē' ('dance, O snake!'), addressed to the snake: praise of Śiva and the guru, the impermanence and filth of the body, the uselessness of learning, caste and ritual for liberation, and the inner ascent. Later readers take the snake as the coiled power (kuṇṭali) within.

scholarly.text: undetermined; the Siddhar song corpus is usually placed c. 1400–1800

structure.description: c. 130 stanzas (count recalled at low confidence)

notes: Not in the local e-text set. The snake=kuṇṭali reading is an interpretation, recorded as such.

summary: Paippalāda asks the Lord what arose first; Maheśa answers with the five faces of Śiva (Sadyojāta, Aghora, Vāmadeva, Tatpuruṣa, Īśāna) and their correspondences; later verses, addressed to Śākala, teach the five-syllable mantra and Śiva in the cave of the heart.

title: Pañcadaśī

attribution.tradition: Vidyāraṇya; some accounts ascribe part of the work to Bhāratītīrtha
attribution.scholarly: Vidyāraṇya (with possible co-authorship)

structure.description: 15 chapters in three groups of five

summary: Vidyāraṇya's fifteen-chapter verse manual in three pentads — five 'discriminations' (viveka: of reality, the elements, the sheaths, duality, the great sayings), five 'lamps' (dīpa: the picture, contentment, the immutable, meditation, the theatre) and five 'blisses' (ānanda: of yoga, of the self, of non-duality, of knowledge, of objects). It distinguishes māyā (pure sattva) as the adjunct of Īśvara from avidyā (impure sattva) as the adjunct of the jīva, and gives the canvas, four-space, tenth-man and theatre-lamp illustrations and the seven states of the jīva.

title: Pañcakalpa
summary: A Chedasūtra on monastic conduct counted in some old lists (instead of the Jītakalpa); the root text is lost, and only a bhāṣya and cūrṇi material are known (low confidence).

title: Pañcapādikā

attribution.tradition: Padmapāda; the name 'five pādas' and the tradition that the rest was destroyed (his uncle burnt the manuscript, Śaṅkaradigvijaya) explain why only the opening survives
attribution.scholarly: Padmapāda (8th c.)

summary: Padmapāda's commentary on the adhyāsa-bhāṣya and the first four sūtras of Śaṅkara's BSBh: analyses the definition of superimposition, presents ignorance as an insentient power (avidyā-śakti) that is the material cause of superimposition, glosses 'mithyā' as 'indescribable', and treats the jīva as a reflection of Brahman in the ego.

title: Pañcapādikāvivaraṇa
summary: Prakāśātman's sub-commentary on the Pañcapādikā, founding text of the Vivaraṇa school: Brahman is the locus and object of a positive (bhāva-rūpa) indescribable ignorance, established by perception, inference and presumption; the jīva is the reflection of Brahman, real and identical with its prototype; hearing is the principal means, enjoined by a restrictive injunction; the mahāvākya yields immediate knowledge.

title: Pañcapadyāni
summary: Five verses on the kinds of listeners to the Lord's stories.

title: Pañcaprakriyā
summary: A short work by Sarvajñātman on five topics of Advaita method.

title: Pāñcarātrarakṣā

editions.name: ed. M. Duraiswami Aiyangar and T. Venugopalacharya, Adyar (Muktabodha M00040)

summary: Vedānta Deśika's defence of the Pāñcarātra and exposition of its ritual, building on Yāmuna.

title: Pañcārthabhāṣya
alt_titles: Kauṇḍinya's commentary on the Pāśupata Sūtra

attribution.tradition: 'Composed by the revered Kauṇḍinya' (colophon of each adhyāya).

title: Paraśurāma Kalpasūtra
summary: The ritual code of Śrīvidyā in sūtra form, in ten sections: initiation, the worship of Gaṇapati, the preliminaries (Śrīkrama), the worship of Lalitā, the nine-enclosure worship of the Śrīcakra, the worship of Śyāmā, of Vārāhī and of Parā, fire offering, and rules common to all. It opens with a statement of doctrine and conduct (the thirty-six principles, the jīva as Śiva covered, self-awareness as the goal, faith in the tradition) and calls itself a great Upaniṣad of the Traipura doctrine.

attribution.tradition: Composed by Paraśurāma Bhārgava, chief disciple of Mahādeva (colophon); tradition also links it to Dattātreya's teaching.
attribution.scholarly: anonymous; date uncertain, before the 18th c.

title: Parātrīśikā
summary: A short Kaula-Trika dialogue: the Goddess asks how the Unsurpassed (anuttara) grants immediate Kaula perfection. Bhairava teaches the emanation of the letters as the tattvas (vv. 5-9), the Heart of Bhairava as the 'third Brahman' (10), the powers of reciting and remembering it (11-20), the tattvas from Kālāgni to Śiva (21-23), the universe resting in the Heart-seed as a banyan tree in its seed (24), initiation for one who knows this (25), and a worship procedure (26-33). It closes 'this is the Rudrayāmala' (35).

attribution.tradition: Spoken by Bhairava; presents itself as belonging to the Rudrayāmala (final verse).
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous; transmitted in Kashmir with the commentaries of Abhinavagupta and others.

title: Parimēlaḻakar's commentary on the Tirukkuṟaḷ

title: Paripāṭal
summary: One of the eight Saṅgam anthologies (Eṭṭuttokai): hymns in the paripāṭal metre, of which about two dozen survive, several to Tirumāl (Viṣṇu), others to Cevvēḷ (Murukaṉ) and the river Vaiyai; its Tirumāl hymns praise him as the source and substance of all things and name his hill-shrine Tirumāliruñcōlai. A precursor of Āḻvār devotion, not an Āḻvār text.
notes: Placed with lin:alvar as the earliest Tamil devotional hymns to Tirumāl; it belongs to Saṅgam literature, for which no lineage entry exists. Many poets; attributions per hymn are given in the colophons and not recorded here.

summary: The root text of the Pāśupatas. Adhyāya 1 prescribes the first-stage observance in the temple (ash-bathing thrice daily, lying in ash, wearing the used garland, the six-limbed offering of laughter, song, dance, the ḍuṇḍuṅkāra sound, prostration and muttering) and lists the powers that arise; adhyāyas 2-4 teach worship of Rudra alone, courting dishonour by feigned madness and the transfer of merit and sin, and non-return; adhyāya 5 teaches the solitary yogin in empty houses, caves and cremation grounds, meditation on Oṃ in the heart, constant remembrance of Rudra and the end of suffering by the Lord's grace.

The Sthānāṅga, Samavāyāṅga and Nandī describe a different original content (questions and answers, including on spells and prognostication); the commentators note the difference.

attribution.scholarly: Anonymous compilation with layers of different ages, fixed in writing at Valabhī in the 5th c. CE.

notes: Why the content changed is not recorded with certainty; later tradition says the original was withdrawn because its magical content could be misused (low confidence).

Books 2–7 are the family books: 2 Gṛtsamada, 3 Viśvāmitra, 4 Vāmadeva, 5 Atri, 6 Bharadvāja, 7 Vasiṣṭha; book 8 chiefly the Kāṇvas (and Āṅgirasas); book 9 the hymns to Soma Pavamāna gathered from all families; books 1 and 10 are collections of many seers and are regarded as later. A second division into 8 aṣṭakas × 8 adhyāyas (64 adhyāyas) and vargas is used for recitation.

Most traditional and modern readings of the Ṛgveda start from it.

title: Ṛgveda Padapāṭha
summary: The word-by-word recitation of the Ṛgveda, ascribed to Śākalya, which undoes the euphonic combinations (sandhi) and marks compound members, so that every word and accent of the continuous text is fixed; it is the basis of the krama and other interwoven recitations and the oldest witness to how the tradition understood each word.

attribution.scholarly: the Padapāṭha is very old (pre-Pāṇinian); Śākalya is cited by Yāska and Pāṇini

The omission of 10.121.10 is confirmed (Max Müller, SBE 32: 'not decomposed in the Pada-pāṭha'; the GRETIL Padapāṭha file carries it only in saṃhitā form). The reported omission of the Vālakhilya hymns could NOT be confirmed: web sources only say the Vālakhilya are an appendix, and the GRETIL Padapāṭha does give pada text for 8.49ff. (possibly editorial). Date 'before Yāska and Pāṇini' consistent with sources placing Śākalya c. 700 BCE.

title: Śāradātilaka
summary: U31 contribution (lineage owner): the most authoritative manual of mantra-śāstra. Paṭala 1 gives the cosmogony of sound — Śakti, nāda and bindu from the supreme Lord (1.7), the threefold bindu (1.8–9), śabda-brahman as the consciousness of all beings (1.11–13), dwelling as kuṇḍalinī and manifesting as the letters (1.14) — and the fifty letters with their deities; paṭala 2 gives the classes of mantras, their fifty defects (2.64–70), the ten purifications (2.112–122), and the marks of guru and disciple and the period of testing (2.141–153); later paṭalas give the mantras, worship and puraścaraṇa of many deities, and the last paṭala treats yoga.

title: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Mādhyandina)
summary: The 'Brāhmaṇa of a hundred paths', the great Brāhmaṇa of the White Yajurveda. It explains the whole Śrauta ritual — new- and full-moon, fire establishment, Agnihotra, ancestral offering, seasonal rites, Soma, royal consecration, the fire-altar (Agnicayana, books 6–10, with its 'secret' in book 10), horse, human and all-sacrifice, the funeral mound, the Pravargya — and teaches the sacrifice as the cosmic Person and year: Prajāpati fell apart after emitting creatures and is rebuilt in the altar. It records the teaching of Śāṇḍilya (10.6.3), the debates of Yājñavalkya at Janaka's court, the debts, the five great sacrifices, upanayana, Vedic self-study, the flood, and ends with the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (14.4–9).

title: Śatarudrīya (Śrī Rudram, Rudrādhyāya)

Its eighth section contains 'namaḥ śivāya ca śivatarāya ca', the source the Śaiva traditions give for the five-syllable formula.
notes: Used in the agnicayana to pacify Rudra; recited in the tradition as Rudra-japa (Ekādaśa-, Laghu-, Mahā-, Atirudra) and in Śaiva worship. The Jābāla Upaniṣad names śatarudrīya recitation as a means to immortality (reference only).

title: Saundaryalaharī
summary: A hymn of one hundred verses to the Goddess. The first part (verses 1-41, called the Ānandalaharī) teaches the doctrine: Śiva can act only when joined to Śakti, the Goddess's ascent through the six cakras and return as kuṇḍalinī, the structure of the Śrīcakra, the coded Śrīvidyā mantra, the Goddess as Śiva's body, and her presence in each cakra; the second part describes her beauty from crown to foot and ends by offering the hymn made of her own words back to her.

attribution.tradition: Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda. In the common legend Śaṅkara received a hymn of a hundred verses at Kailāsa; Nandin (in other versions Gaṇeśa) snatched it, leaving the first forty-one, and Śaṅkara composed the rest.
attribution.scholarly: Authorship by the Advaita teacher of the Brahma Sūtra commentary is doubted; the text is well established by the time of its 16th-c. commentators.

summary: An Upāṅga on astronomy and calendar: the motions of the two suns and two moons of Jambūdvīpa, the lunar mansions and the five-year yuga; nearly identical in content with the Candraprajñapti.
notes: Lists differ on the order of the Sūrya-, Jambūdvīpa- and Candra-prajñaptis (5th–7th Upāṅgas).

title: Suśruta Saṃhitā

attribution.tradition: Dhanvantari, born as King Divodāsa of Kāśī, taught Suśruta and his fellow students (Su Sū 1.3-21); Ḍalhaṇa reports that Nāgārjuna redacted the text.
attribution.scholarly: Compiled in layers; the Uttaratantra is a later supplement; final form before c. 6th c. CE.

tradition.text: teaching of Dhanvantari-Divodāsa at Kāśī

scholarly.text: core perhaps c. 2nd c. BCE onward; final redaction c. 3rd–6th c. CE

structure.description: Five sthānas of 120 chapters (Sūtra 46, Nidāna 16, Śārīra 10, Cikitsā 40, Kalpa 8) plus the Uttaratantra (66 chapters) — Su Sū 1.39-40

summary: The foundational compendium of the surgeons' school: the origin and eight limbs of Āyurveda, surgery and its instruments, the doṣas, dhātus and malas and the definition of health (Sū 15.41), the stages of disease (Sū 21), a Sāṃkhya account of creation and of the person (Śā 1), embryology, anatomy and the 107 marmas (Śā 6), therapeutics, rejuvenation, toxicology, and in the Uttaratantra eye, ear and head diseases, children's diseases, the seizing spirits (Utt 60) and the devices of exposition (Utt 65).

editions.name: ed. Jādavji Trikamji Ācārya with Ḍalhaṇa's Nibandhasaṃgraha (Bombay 1938 and reprints)

title: Sūta Gītā

title: Sūtrakṛtāṅga
summary: The second Aṅga, largely polemical: it states and rejects the views of other teachers (materialists, the one-self doctrine, the soul-is-the-body doctrine, non-agency, fatalism, Buddhist momentariness), classifies all rival doctrines under four heads (kriyāvāda, akriyāvāda, ajñānavāda, vinayavāda), warns the monk against temptations, praises Mahāvīra, and in Book II gives the parable of the lotus, Ārdraka's debates with rival ascetics and the Nālandā dialogue with a follower of Pārśva.

attribution.tradition: The meaning (artha) was taught by Mahāvīra; the gaṇadhara Sudharman composed the sūtras and transmitted them to Jambū ('suyaṃ me āusaṃ…', 'I have heard, O long-lived one'); redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous compilation with layers of different ages, fixed in writing at Valabhī in the 5th c. CE.

scholarly.text: Book I old (verse; often placed c. 3rd–2nd c. BCE), Book II later

structure.description: 2 śrutaskandhas: I = 16 lectures (mostly verse), II = 7 lectures (mostly prose)

summary: Śīlāṅka's Sanskrit commentary on the Sūtrakṛtāṅga, which identifies and explains the rival doctrines the text refutes.

title: Sūtrapāṭh
summary: The sayings of Cakradhar arranged by topic by Keśobās: the four eternal realities (jīva, devatā, prapañca, Parameśvara), the uselessness of worshipping the devatās for liberation, and the conduct of the renunciant (wandering, begging, non-violence, detachment). The Mahānubhāvas' doctrinal scripture.

attribution.tradition: Cakradhar's own words, collected by Keśobās.
attribution.scholarly: Accepted as the earliest digest of Cakradhar's sayings.

structure.description: topical chapters (prakaraṇas) including Vicāra (doctrine) and Ācāra (conduct); exact chapter list and sūtra count to verify

title: Sūtrārthabodhinī
summary: A brief commentary by Nārāyaṇatīrtha, written at Prayāga (closing verse). Its introduction: liberation is the highest human aim, reached through hearing, reflection and deep contemplation; Patañjali composed the sūtras in four pādas; Bādarāyaṇa (Vyāsa) wrote the bhāṣya.

title: Sutta Nipāta
summary: A collection of 71 (72 by some counts) verse suttas in five vaggas — Uraga, Cūḷa, Mahā, Aṭṭhaka, Pārāyana — including the Mettā, Ratana and Maṅgala suttas, the Padhāna (the bodhisatta's struggle with Māra), the Vāseṭṭha (true brahmin), and the Aṭṭhakavagga and Pārāyanavagga, counted among the oldest Buddhist poetry.

structure.description: 5 vaggas: Uraga (12), Cūḷa (14), Mahā (12), Aṭṭhaka (16), Pārāyana (intro + 16 questions + epilogue)

scholarly.text: Aṭṭhaka- and Pārāyanavagga among the oldest strata (commented on in the canonical Niddesa); the collection as a whole later

editions.licence: CC0 / public domain as published by SuttaCentral

title: Sutta Piṭaka
summary: The basket of discourses: the Buddha's and his great disciples' teachings arranged in five collections (nikāya) by length (Dīgha, Majjhima), by topic (Saṃyutta), by number (Aṅguttara), and a miscellany (Khuddaka).

structure.description: Dīgha Nikāya (34 suttas), Majjhima Nikāya (152), Saṃyutta Nikāya (56 saṃyuttas), Aṅguttara Nikāya (11 nipātas), Khuddaka Nikāya (15 to 18 books by edition)

tradition.text: recited by Ānanda at the First Council

scholarly.text: c. 5th–3rd c. BCE for the core; some Khuddaka books to the 1st c. BCE or later

title: Suttavibhaṅga
summary: The 'analysis of the rules': each Pātimokkha rule with the story of the incident that led the Buddha to lay it down, the rule itself, a word-commentary, the variations and the non-offence cases.

structure.description: Mahāvibhaṅga (the 227 bhikkhu rules) and Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga (the rules particular to nuns; of 311 bhikkhunī rules only those not shared with monks are analysed in full)

title: Svabodhodayamañjarī
summary: Vāmanadatta's short verse text (45 verses) on the rise of self-awareness through non-dual contemplation.

structure.description: 45 verses

title: Svacchandatantra (Svacchandabhairavatantra)
summary: A principal Mantrapīṭha tantra of the Bhairava corpus, centred on Svacchandabhairava (Aghora) and Aghoreśvarī; the mainstay of Kashmirian Śaiva ritual (worship, initiation), with a large cosmography of the worlds (bhuvanas) and teachings on yoga and the subtle body. Kṣemarāja's Uddyota reads it in the light of non-dual doctrine.

attribution.tradition: Revealed by Bhairava to the Goddess.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous; widely cited from the 9th c.

structure.description: 15 paṭalas

title: Svacchandoddyota
summary: Kṣemarāja's commentary on the Svacchandatantra, reading its ritual and cosmology non-dually.

title: Svārājyasiddhi
summary: Gaṅgādharendra Sarasvatī's verse treatise (with auto-commentary) on attaining 'self-sovereignty' — liberation as the self's rule over itself.

title: Svaramelakalānidhi of Rāmāmātya
summary: Rāmāmātya's treatise classifying rāgas under parent scales (mela).

title: Svāyambhuvāgama

attribution.tradition: revealed by Sadāśiva from the upper (Īśāna) face; first received by Nidhana, then Nalinodbhava (Brahmā) (Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92; Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10)
attribution.scholarly: texts now transmitted under this title are mostly South Indian redactions centred on temple ritual; their relation to the early scripture of the same name is not established here

structure.description: Rudrabheda no. 13 in the Kāmika's order; 3 upabhedas in the Kāmika's list

notes: Kiraṇa 10.16/10.24: Nidhana → Padmasambhava. Śrīkaṇṭhīya: 'Svayambhuva'. In the Kāmika's image of the scriptures as Sadāśiva's body it is the two breasts (pūrva 1.93–101). Lists checked by the Phase-B author against local e-texts: Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/Kamikagama.md (Kāmika Pūrvabhāga, Madras 1909 Grantha ed. as transcribed)), Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10.3–27 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/kiranagama.md (Kiraṇa vidyāpāda, South Indian printed text as transcribed)) and the Śrīkaṇṭhīya list quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)).
summary: No. 13 of the 28 Śaiva Siddhānta mūlāgamas (Rudrabheda). According to the Kāmika it was first received by Nidhana, then Nalinodbhava (Brahmā). The Kāmika assigns it 3 upabheda(s): Prajāpatimata, Padma, Svāyambhuva. An early 'Svāyambhuva' survives as the Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṅgraha (src:svayambhuvasutrasangraha); later South Indian material under the title is not assessed here.

title: Śvetāmbara Āgamas (the Jain canon)
summary: The canonical scriptures of the Śvetāmbara Jains: the twelve-limbed 'basket of the gaṇin' (duvālasaṅga gaṇipiḍaga) of which eleven Aṅgas survive, together with the 'outside the limbs' (aṅgabāhya) texts. Mūrtipūjakas count forty-five texts (11 Aṅgas, 12 Upāṅgas, 10 Prakīrṇakas, 6 Chedasūtras, 4 Mūlasūtras, 2 Cūlikāsūtras); Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs accept thirty-two. The Digambaras hold that the original Aṅgas were lost and do not accept this collection.

attribution.tradition: The Aṅgas go back to the gaṇadharas' composition of Mahāvīra's teaching; the aṅgabāhya texts to later elders (sthaviras); recited at the councils of Pāṭaliputra, Mathurā and Valabhī and written down at Valabhī under Devarddhigaṇi (980 or 993 years after the nirvāṇa).
attribution.scholarly: Compiled from materials of very different ages (c. 4th c. BCE – 5th c. CE); the grouping into Upāṅgas, Chedas, Mūlas and Prakīrṇakas and the count of 45 are medieval (the Nandī classifies differently: aṅga-praviṣṭa / aṅga-bāhya, kālika / utkālika).

tradition.text: taught by Mahāvīra (d. 527 BCE by the traditional reckoning); written down at Valabhī 453 or 466 CE

scholarly.text: oldest layers c. 4th–3rd c. BCE; closed in the 5th c. CE

structure.description: 45 texts (Mūrtipūjaka) or 32 (Sthānakavāsī, Terāpanthī); see cpt:svetambara-canon-45 and cpt:sthanakavasi-canon-32

title: Taittirīya Āraṇyaka
summary: The Āraṇyaka of the Taittirīya Black Yajurveda: the Āruṇaketuka fire-altar (1); the book of Vedic self-study with the twilight worship, the wind-girdled seers who were śramaṇas (2.7) and the five great sacrifices (2.10); the cāturhotra altar (3); the Pravargya mantras and explanation (4–5); the funeral and ancestral mantras (6); the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (7–9); and the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad (10), which contains the mantras of the food-offering into the breaths.

title: Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa
summary: The Brāhmaṇa of the Taittirīya school of the Black Yajurveda, supplementing the Saṃhitā's own prose: fire establishment, Agnihotra, Soma and royal rites, the nakṣatra offerings, the horse sacrifice, the cosmogony of Prajāpati diving as a boar to raise the earth (1.1.3), and the three Kāṭhaka chapters (3.10–12) on the Sāvitra, Nāciketa and Vaiśvasṛja fire-altars — including Naciketas' visit to Death (3.11.8), Bharadvāja's three lives of Vedic study (3.10.11) and the cosmic session of the world-creators (3.12.9).

attribution.tradition: the Taittirīya school, named after Tittiri (or, in the Purāṇic story, after the partridges (tittiri) who picked up the Yajus disgorged by Yājñavalkya)

summary: The Prātiśākhya of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (Black Yajurveda): production and classification of sounds, sandhi, accents and the relation of the continuous to the word-by-word text.

title: Tantrāloka
summary: Abhinavagupta's encyclopaedic exposition of the Trika on the basis of the Mālinīvijayottara, integrating Kaula and Krama. After defining bondage as ignorance and knowledge as the sole cause of liberation (1.22-23), it orders all Śaiva practice by the four means (chs. 2-5), sets out time, space, the tattvas and the paths of manifestation (6-12), the descent of grace (13), the whole ritual of initiation, consecration, funerary and daily rites (14-28), the secret Kula ritual (29), mantra, maṇḍala and mudrā (30-32), and ends with unification, the harmony of the scriptures, the lineage and the author's account of himself (33-37).

structure.description: 37 āhnikas (chapters), c. 5,800 verses; chapter topics per Abhinavagupta's own table of contents (TĀ 1.278-329) and colophons: 1 vijñānabheda (the kinds of knowledge; knowledge as the cause of liberation; table of contents); 2 anupāya (the means-less); 3 śāmbhavopāya (the reflection of the universe in consciousness; the letters); 4 śāktopāya (purification of thought, sattarka, the wheel of consciousness, the twelve Kālīs, critique of rules); 5 āṇavopāya (meditation, uccāra of prāṇa, the seven ānandas, the five signs, karaṇa, varṇa); 6 kālopāya / kālatattva (time in the breath and its cycles); 7 cakrodaya (the arising of the wheels; mantra and breath counts); 8 deśādhvan (the path of space: the worlds); 9 tattvādhvan (the path of the tattvas); 10 tattvabheda (divisions of the tattvas; the states and the seven pramātṛs); 11 kalādhvan (the path of the kalās; letters and mantras); 12 adhvopayoga (use of the paths); 13 śaktipāta (the descent of power; its grades); 14 dīkṣopakrama (preliminaries of initiation; removal of concealment); 15 samayadīkṣā (initiation into the samaya; the samaya rules); 16 prameya (the putraka initiation and the knowables purified); 17 vikṣipta/extended initiation (cord, purification of the tattvas, burning the bonds); 18 saṅkṣiptadīkṣā (abbreviated initiation); 19 sadyaḥsamutkrānti (initiation bringing immediate departure from the body); 20 tulādīkṣā (initiation by the balance); 21 parokṣadīkṣā (initiation of the absent and the dead); 22 liṅgoddhāra (removal of a prior sectarian mark); 23 abhiṣeka (consecration as teacher or adept); 24 antyeṣṭi (final rites); 25 śrāddha (rites for the dead); 26 sthaṇḍilapūjā (daily worship on a ritual ground; the remaining life of the initiate); 27 liṅgārcā (worship of the liṅga); 28 parva-pavitraka etc. (occasional rites; the gathering of yoginīs; rites for the guru); 29 rahasyavidhi (the secret Kula ritual); 30 mantra (the mantras); 31 maṇḍala; 32 mudrā; 33 ekīkāra (unification of the paths); 34 svarūpapraveśa (entry into one's own nature); 35 śāstrasammelana (the harmony of the scriptures); 36 āyātikrama (the descent of the scripture through the lineage); 37 upādeyabhāva (why this scripture is to be accepted; the author's account of himself)

summary: The twelve-book canon of Tamil Śaiva sacred literature: (1–3) Tiruñāṉacampantar's hymns; (4–6) Tirunāvukkaracar's (Appar's) hymns; (7) Cuntarar's hymns — books 1–7 together are the Tēvāram; (8) Māṇikkavācakar's Tiruvācakam and Tirukkōvaiyār; (9) the Tiruvicaippā of nine poets and Cēntaṉār's Tiruppallāṇṭu; (10) Tirumūlar's Tirumantiram; (11) forty works by twelve poets (Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār, Cēramāṉ Perumāḷ, Nakkīrar, Paṭṭiṉattup Piḷḷaiyār, Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi and others); (12) Cēkkiḻār's Periya Purāṇam.

attribution.scholarly: compiled in stages c. 10th–12th c.; the identity of the king and the exact stages are debated

scholarly.text: contents c. 6th–12th c.; compilation c. 10th–12th c.

By tradition the text through which Parāśara Bhaṭṭar won over the Advaitin who became Nañjīyar, hence recited at the opening of the recitation festival.

attribution.tradition: Tukārām's; his notebooks, thrown into the Indrāyaṇī at Rāmeśvar Bhaṭṭ's order, rose dry after thirteen days; Santājī Jagnāḍe and others wrote them down.

summary: Kṛṣṇa instructs Uddhava to renounce attachment, see the world as the Lord's māyā and wander with equal vision. Through the story of Yadu and a young avadhūta brāhmaṇa it teaches learning from twenty-four teachers in nature, then expounds bondage and liberation, holy company, the guṇas, meditation on the Lord, the eighteen siddhis as obstacles, the three yogas of knowledge, action and devotion by disposition, the tattvas, worship (kriyā-yoga), and devotion as the easiest and highest path.

summary: Kṛṣṇa teaches Arjuna the knowledge of Brahman together with yogic anatomy (the nāḍīs, suṣumnā, brahmarandhra): the knower of Brahman, satisfied with the nectar of knowledge, has nothing more to do; the self is to be known beyond scripture, which is left behind like husk once the grain is taken.
notes: Distinct from the Anugītā (Mahābhārata 14.16-50), which is also a post-war teaching to Arjuna.

title: Uttarādhyayana-Śiṣyahitā of Śāntisūri

title: Uttarādhyayana-Sukhabodhā
summary: Devendragaṇi (Nemicandra)'s commentary on the Uttarādhyayana (1073 CE), prized for its Prakrit stories illustrating each chapter.

title: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra
summary: The first Mūlasūtra, thirty-six chapters of verse and some prose: discipline toward the teacher, the twenty-two hardships, the four rare things, the ignorant and the wise death, the renunciation of Nami, the leaf of the tree ('Gautama, be not careless for a moment'), the outcaste monk Harikeśa, Nemi and Rājīmatī, the dialogue of Keśin and Gautama, the eight 'mothers of the doctrine', the true brāhmaṇa, the path to liberation, austerities, the kinds of karma, the six leśyās and the classes of living and non-living things. Tradition holds that Mahāvīra recited it in his last hours.

attribution.tradition: Mahāvīra's last teaching, given without being asked before his nirvāṇa at Pāvā (Utt 36 end)

title: Vacana literature (vacana sāhitya)
summary: The corpus of vacanas — short rhythmic Kannada prose-poems, usually closing with the author's signature name (aṅkita) for the Lord — composed by the twelfth-century śaraṇas of Kalyāṇa and by later vacanakāras. They teach devotion to Śiva as the liṅga, the six stages (ṣaṭsthala), the triad of guru, liṅga and jaṅgama, work as worship (kāyaka) and giving (dāsōha), and criticize caste, pollution rules, temple and Vedic ritualism and outward show in favour of lived experience (anubhava).

attribution.tradition: the utterances of the śaraṇas (Basava, Allama Prabhu, Akka Mahādēvi, Cennabasava and some two hundred others, women among them), preserved in palm-leaf bundles and carried to Uḷavi after the Kalyāṇa upheaval
attribution.scholarly: a twelfth-century core with later accretions; much of the corpus is known through fifteenth–sixteenth-century Vijayanagara-period anthologies

tradition.text: 12th c. (the śaraṇa generation of Kalyāṇa)

scholarly.text: 12th-c. core; later vacanakāras to the 17th–18th c.

title: Vādāvalī

title: Vādhūla Śrautasūtra

title: Vaiśeṣika Sūtra

attribution.tradition: Composed by the sage Kaṇāda (Kaṇabhuj, Ulūka, Kāśyapa).
attribution.scholarly: A layered text transmitted in divergent recensions; the recension commented on by Candrānanda is older than that of Śaṅkara Miśra's Upaskāra, which contains sūtras absent from it (e.g. Upaskāra 1.1.4 listing the six categories).

tradition.text: ancient; the sage Kaṇāda

scholarly.text: core perhaps c. 1st c. BCE – 1st c. CE (estimates vary widely); extant recensions redacted later

structure.description: 10 adhyāyas; in Candrānanda's recension books 1–8 have two āhnikas (book 8 one) and books 9–10 none; c. 370–385 sūtras depending on recension. Teaching ids in this unit use Candrānanda's numbering (DCS e-text); Upaskāra numbers are noted where known.

summary: The root text of Vaiśeṣika in ten books. It announces the explanation of dharma — that from which prosperity and the highest good result — and grounds the Veda's authority; lists the nine substances, the qualities and the five motions and defines substance, quality and motion; treats being, universals and particulars, the elements, time, space, the self (with its marks and plurality) and the atomic mind; atoms and perception; motions caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa); yoga and liberation; ethics of giving, food and ritual observances; inherence; absence; perception, inference and memory; and the seers' knowledge.

title: Vaiyākaraṇa-bhūṣaṇa-sāra of Kauṇḍa Bhaṭṭa
summary: The abridged Bhūṣaṇa, studied as the standard introduction to grammatical philosophy; its sections (nirṇaya) treat the meaning of roots, verbal endings, case endings, stems, compounds, the power of words (śakti), particles, and close with the settlement of the sphoṭa (sphoṭa-nirṇaya).

title: Vaiyākaraṇa-siddhānta-kārikā of Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita
summary: Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita's short verse summary of the grammarians' doctrines on the meanings of roots, endings, nominal stems, compounds and negation, ending with the sphoṭa, where he holds that on final analysis only the sentence-sphoṭa is real.

title: Vaiyākaraṇa-siddhānta-mañjūṣā (Bṛhanmañjūṣā) of Nāgeśa

title: Vaiyāsikanyāyamālā

title: Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (Mādhyandina)
summary: The White Yajurveda Saṃhitā: the adhvaryu's formulas and verses without explanatory prose (which is given separately in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa). Its forty adhyāyas run through the new- and full-moon rites, agnihotra and seasonal rites, the soma sacrifice, the royal rites, the fire altar (11–18, with the Śatarudrīya in 16), the sautrāmaṇī and the horse sacrifice (22–25), then supplementary books with the Puruṣa Sūkta (31), the hymn of the One (32), the Śivasaṅkalpa verses on mind (34.1–6), the funeral (35), peace chants (36) and the pravargya, and closes with the Īśa Upaniṣad (40).

summary: 'Who is a brāhmaṇa?' — not the jīva, not the body, not birth, not learning, not ritual action nor dharmic deeds; a brāhmaṇa is one who has directly realized the non-dual Self and is free of faults, desire and pride; this is the intent of śruti, smṛti, itihāsa and purāṇa.

title: Vāk Sūkta (Devī Sūkta, Ṛgveda 10.125)
summary: Speech (Vāc) proclaims herself: she moves with the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas and All-gods and bears Mitra-Varuṇa, Indra-Agni and the Aśvins; she is the queen, the gatherer of treasures, first of those worthy of worship, placed by the gods in many places; through her one eats, sees, breathes and hears, and those who do not know her dwell beside her; whom she loves she makes formidable, a brahman, a seer, a sage; she bends Rudra's bow; she gives birth to the father on the world's head; her womb is in the waters; she blows forth like the wind, beyond heaven and earth.

title: Vākyapadīya
summary: Bhartṛhari's treatise on 'sentence and word' in three books. Book 1 (Brahmakāṇḍa) teaches that Brahman is the Word-principle appearing as the world, that all cognition is word-permeated, the sphoṭa–dhvani distinction, the three levels of speech and grammar as a path to liberation; book 2 (Vākyakāṇḍa) argues that the sentence is the indivisible unit of meaning, grasped as pratibhā; book 3 (Padakāṇḍa or Prakīrṇaka) analyses universals, substance, relation, quality, direction, means, action, time, person, number, gender and compounds in fourteen sections (samuddeśa).

attribution.tradition: Bhartṛhari (often identified in the tradition with the poet of the Śatakatraya)
attribution.scholarly: Bhartṛhari the grammarian; his identity with the poet of the Śatakas is doubted

title: Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtra
summary: A Dharmasūtra associated with the Ṛgveda. It places dharma in śruti and smṛti and, failing these, in the practice of the cultured, 'one free of desire' (1.4–6); teaches that the Vedas do not purify one without right conduct, and leave him at death as fledglings leave the nest (6.3); lets a student who has kept his vow enter whichever order he wishes (7.1–3); tells the renouncer to give up all rites but never the Veda (10.4); and ends: 'practise dharma, not adharma; speak truth, not untruth; look far, not near; look to the highest, not to what is not highest' (30.1).

summary: An eight-limbed yoga for the twice-born framed by Vedic orthodoxy: yamas and niyamas, a few postures, the channels and kuṇḍalinī, breath-control, a withdrawal (pratyāhāra) that moves the breath through the eighteen vital points (marma), concentration on the elements, meditation and samādhi. It is among the early texts that teach kuṇḍalinī outside a tantric frame and is named as an authority on postures in HYP 1.18.

It declares that the Vedas exist for the sacrifices, the sacrifices depend on time, and so this science of time stands at the head of the Vedāṅgas.

title: Vedāntasāra

summary: Sadānanda's standard primer: the four preliminaries (qualified student, subject, relation, purpose); superimposition and retraction; ignorance with its two powers, collective and individual, and the three bodies, states and sheaths; quintuplication; a graded refutation of mistaken views of the self; the analysis of 'tat tvam asi' by exclusive-inclusive implication; hearing, reflection, contemplation and samādhi with eight auxiliaries and four obstacles; the jīvanmukta.

title: Vedāntasāra (of Rāmānuja)

title: Vijñānabhairava
summary: A dialogue in which the Goddess (Bhairavī) asks Bhairava about his true nature; he rejects every form 'with parts' (the ninefold, the mass of sounds, the three-headed, nāda-bindu...) as a device for the confused (vv. 7-13), describes the supreme state as indescribable fullness identical with the Goddess (14-21), and in answer to her request for means (22-23) teaches 112 contemplations (dhāraṇā) of the 'waveless state' (24-138; counted at 139). It then redefines japa, meditation, worship, oblation, sacrifice and bathing as inner acts (144-153), teaches the natural 'haṃsa' repetition of the breath (154-156), enjoins secrecy (157-160), and closes with the Goddess embracing Śiva, having grasped 'the essence of the Rudrayāmala' (161-163).

attribution.tradition: Spoken by Bhairava to Bhairavī; claims to be the essence of the Rudrayāmala and of the Trika (vv. 1, 161-162).
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous. The claimed Rudrayāmala origin cannot be verified: the early Rudrayāmala is lost, and the extant Rudrayāmala (Uttaratantra) is a different and later text. Cited by Kṣemarāja, who began a commentary on it.

tradition.text: Part of the revealed Rudrayāmala.

title: Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra)

attribution.tradition: By Vyāsa, identified with Veda-Vyāsa and with Bādarāyaṇa (Vijñānabhikṣu, Yogavārttika intro. and 1.1; Nārāyaṇatīrtha, Sūtrārthabodhinī intro.).
attribution.scholarly: The author's identity is unknown; Maas (following Bronkhorst and others) holds that sūtra and bhāṣya are one work by Patañjali; older scholarship placed the bhāṣya well after the sūtras. The bhāṣya cites 'Patañjali' by name once (3.44), a point used in this debate.

scholarly.text: c. 325–425 CE if one work with the sūtras (Maas); older estimates placed it later (6th–8th c.)

structure.description: running prose commentary on all 195 sūtras, headed by a maṅgala verse to the lord of serpents; each pāda closes 'iti śrīpātañjale sāṃkhyapravacane yogaśāstre ... vyāsabhāṣye'

summary: The oldest and authoritative commentary. It defines yoga as samādhi and names the five levels of mind (1.1); analyzes the vṛttis, the kleśas and their states (with a fifth, 'burnt-seed' state), karma and its fruition; gives the fourfold scheme modelled on medicine (2.15) and the sevenfold final insight (2.27); lists seated postures (2.46); explains saṃyama and the powers, the four kinds of yogin and the invitation of the celestials (3.51), and a detailed cosmology (3.26); and argues against Buddhist views of a momentary mind and of objects as mind-only (1.32, 4.14–24).

title: Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali

attribution.tradition: Composed by Patañjali as a re-teaching (anuśāsana, 1.1) of the yoga first taught by Hiraṇyagarbha (Vijñānabhikṣu, Rāmānanda Sarasvatī, Nāgeśa on 1.1); Patañjali is regarded as an incarnation of Śeṣa (Ananta), the lord of serpents, and identified with the grammarian of the Mahābhāṣya.
attribution.scholarly: Most scholars doubt that the Yoga author is the grammarian (c. 2nd c. BCE). Philipp A. Maas argues, following earlier arguments by J. Bronkhorst, that sūtras and bhāṣya form one work — the Pātañjala Yogaśāstra, as the colophons ('pātañjale sāṃkhyapravacane yogaśāstre') call it — by one author, c. 325–425 CE; others treat the sūtras as older than the bhāṣya.

tradition.text: not dated by the tradition (Patañjali as an incarnation of Śeṣa)

scholarly.text: c. 325–425 CE together with the bhāṣya (Maas); earlier proposals range from the 2nd c. BCE to the 5th c. CE

structure.description: 4 pādas: Samādhi (51 sūtras), Sādhana (55), Vibhūti (55), Kaivalya (34) = 195 sūtras in the Vyāsa-based vulgate (Ānandāśrama ed., and every local commentary e-text). Some editions count 196 by treating 'etena śabdādy antardhānam uktam' — part of the bhāṣya on 3.21 in the Ānandāśrama ed. — as a separate sūtra 3.22, shifting the later numbers of pāda 3 by one. This unit uses the 195-sūtra numbering.

summary: The root text of the Yoga darśana. It defines yoga as the stilling of the activities of the mind (1.2); teaches practice and dispassion, devotion to Īśvara and Oṃ, the obstacles and their remedies, the samāpattis and the kinds of samādhi (pāda 1); kriyā-yoga, the five afflictions, karma, the seer and the seen, and the first five of the eight limbs (pāda 2); concentration, meditation, samādhi, saṃyama, the transformations of mind and the powers with their warnings (pāda 3); and the sources of powers, karma and latent tendencies, the reality of objects, the non-self-luminosity of mind, the cloud of dharma and kaivalya (pāda 4).

title: Yoga Vāsiṣṭha

attribution.tradition: composed by Vālmīki, author of the Rāmāyaṇa, and told to Bharadvāja: the dialogue in which Vasiṣṭha teaches Rāma, with Viśvāmitra present, at Daśaratha's court
attribution.scholarly: the vulgate is a Vedāntic revision of the Kashmiri Mokṣopāya (src:moksopaya), an anonymous 10th-c. philosophical poem; its non-dualism is close to but not identical with Śaṅkara's Advaita and shares vocabulary with Kashmiri Śaiva and Buddhist idealist thought

tradition.text: composed by Vālmīki; the teaching given by Vasiṣṭha to the young Rāma in the Tretā age

scholarly.text: the Kashmiri Mokṣopāya c. 10th c. CE (Slaje, c. 950); the Vedānta-oriented Yoga Vāsiṣṭha vulgate is a later revision (c. 11th-14th c.); older proposals ranged from the 6th to the 13th c.

structure.description: 6 prakaraṇas: Vairāgya (dispassion, 33 sargas), Mumukṣu-vyavahāra (conduct of the seeker, 20), Utpatti (origination, 122), Sthiti (persistence, 62), Upaśama (quiescence, 93), Nirvāṇa (liberation, pūrvārdha 128 + uttarārdha 216). The text names itself Mokṣopāya and claims 32,000 verses (2.17.6); the printed vulgate has roughly 27,000-29,000

summary: Vasiṣṭha teaches the despondent young Rāma that the world is a projection of mind within the one consciousness (cit), arising like a dream; that human effort (pauruṣa) guided by scripture and the good overrides fate, which is only past effort; that liberation comes by inquiry (vicāra) with the four gatekeepers (peace, inquiry, contentment, holy company), by the weakening of latent tendencies (vāsanā) and the stilling of mind and breath, through seven stages of knowledge to liberation while living. The teaching is carried by dozens of stories (Līlā, Karkaṭī, Lavaṇa, Śukra, Dāśūra, Prahlāda, Bali, Gādhi, Uddālaka, Suraghu, Vītahavya, Bhuśuṇḍa, Cūḍālā and Śikhidhvaja, the stone and others).

scholarly.text: Scholarly accounts differ by text. Several Yoga Upaniṣads (e.g. Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kṣurikā, Tejobindu, Nādabindu, Dhyānabindu, Brahmavidyā, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā, Haṃsa) survive in shorter northern versions that are older; the expanded southern recensions (as in this collection) borrow from medieval haṭha works and were probably compiled in South India, perhaps as late as the 18th c. (Bouy 1994).

title: Yogajāgama

attribution.tradition: revealed by Sadāśiva from the upper (Īśāna) face; first received by Sudhā, then Bhasma, then Vibhu (Kiraṇa: Prabhu) (Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92; Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10)
attribution.scholarly: texts now transmitted under this title are mostly South Indian redactions centred on temple ritual; their relation to the early scripture of the same name is not established here

structure.description: Śivabheda no. 2 in the Kāmika's order; 5 upabhedas in the Kāmika's list

editions.name: e-text from a manuscript of M.K.S. Bhattar, Madurai (Muktabodha M00250); IFP MS 39691

notes: Kiraṇa 10.4/10.7: Sudhā → Bhasma → Prabhu. Śrīkaṇṭhīya: 'Yogaja'. In the Kāmika's image of the scriptures as Sadāśiva's body it is the ankles (pūrva 1.93–101). Lists checked by the Phase-B author against local e-texts: Kāmika pūrva 1.30–92 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/Kamikagama.md (Kāmika Pūrvabhāga, Madras 1909 Grantha ed. as transcribed)), Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10.3–27 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/kiranagama.md (Kiraṇa vidyāpāda, South Indian printed text as transcribed)) and the Śrīkaṇṭhīya list quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18 (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)).
summary: No. 2 of the 28 Śaiva Siddhānta mūlāgamas (Śivabheda). According to the Kāmika it was first received by Sudhā, then Bhasma, then Vibhu (Kiraṇa: Prabhu). The Kāmika assigns it 5 upabheda(s): Vīṇāśikhottara, Tāra, Santa, Santati, Ātmayoga. Transmitted in South Indian manuscripts; mainly ritual (kriyā) content.

summary: A short poem in tripadi metre ascribed to Akka Mahādēvi on yoga and the path to the liṅga.

title: Yogarahasya (of Nāthamuni)
summary: Nāthamuni's lost treatise on (aṣṭāṅga) yoga, which the hagiographies say he taught to Kurukai Kāvalappaṉ; the original is lost. A text published in the 20th century under this title is claimed in T. Krishnamacharya's lineage as a recovery; that claim belongs to lin:krishnamacharya and is not accepted here as the original.

tradition.text: Nāthamuni, traditionally 9th–10th c. (hagiographies give an extremely long life)

title: Yogasiddhāntacandrikā
summary: Nārāyaṇatīrtha's extensive vṛtti. Its opening verses give the transmission (Pitāmaha taught yoga; Śeṣa in the sūtras; Vyāsa in the bhāṣya; Vācaspati Miśra and Vijñānabhikṣu clarified the bhāṣya) and argue that Vyāsa's Brahma Sūtras refuted pradhāna's independence, not yoga as meditative cultivation; the introduction treats deep contemplation (nididhyāsana) as samādhi, 'also called rājayoga', and subsumes many named yogas under the eight-limbed yoga.

summary: A vṛtti on the sūtras ('the speech of the lord of serpents') by Sadāśiva Brahmendra, composed, as its closing verses say, by the grace of the teacher and offered at the teacher's feet.

title: Yogasūtradīpikā (Pradīpikā) of Bhāvāgaṇeśa
summary: A commentary 'for the easy understanding of the slow-witted' by Bhāvāgaṇeśa, who says it condenses the meaning examined in the bhāṣya and 'by my teacher himself in the Vārttika' (Vijñānabhikṣu).

title: Yogasūtravṛtti of Nāgeśa (Nāgojī) Bhaṭṭa
summary: A vṛtti on the sūtras by the grammarian Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa. On 1.1 it says the śāstra expounds in detail the yoga taught by Hiraṇyagarbha and others; on 1.2 it glosses citta as the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and nirodha as a special, supersensible effort that dissolves the activities.
notes: Nāgeśa is reported to have written a longer and a shorter vṛtti (Bṛhatī, Laghvī) — which one the local raw_etexts file contains is not verified.

title: Yogavallī
summary: A modern Sanskrit commentary on the Yoga Sūtras. Its introduction surveys the darśanas, gives the count of 195 sūtras (51, 55, 55, 34), notes that some manuscripts mark the end of the work after pāda 3, cites the verse from Bhoja's vṛtti on Patañjali's three kinds of purification, and compares the Vivaraṇa, Tattvavaiśāradī and Yogavārttika on particular sūtras.
notes: Only the Samādhipāda is in the local raw_etexts file; author and date not identified (gap).

title: Yogavārttika

scholarly.text: second half of the 16th c. CE

summary: Vijñānabhikṣu's extensive sub-commentary on the bhāṣya. It calls the bhāṣya 'the essence of all the Veda spoken by Vedavyāsa' and holds Sāṃkhya and the other darśanas to be contained in it like rivers in the ocean (intro.); cites the Yoga-Yājñavalkya for Hiraṇyagarbha as first teacher (1.1); argues for the mutual reflection of consciousness and buddhi against a single-reflection view (1.7); gives its own account of the four samprajñāta samādhis (1.17); and holds that knowledge of the Supreme Lord is the swift cause of liberation (1.51).

editions.name: ed. Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara (Calcutta), with the bhāṣya; e-Bhāratī Sampat e-text

title: Yogaviṣaya
summary: A short tract of thirty-three verses attributed to Mīnanātha (Matsyendra): the qualified disciple, the six centres from ādhāra to ājñā, the three channels, the three knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra, the names of kuṇḍalinī, the nectar raining from the brahma-place, inner worship with the flower of the mind, and the haṃsa repeated 21,600 times as 'so 'ham'.

title: Yogayātrā

title: Yoginīhṛdaya
summary: The esoteric 'heart' of the Vāmakeśvara teaching in three 'codes' (saṅketa): the code of the cakra (the Śrīcakra as the emanation of the supreme Śakti and the universe of principles), the code of the mantra (six levels of the mantra's meaning), and the code of worship (three kinds of worship, inner and outer rites). Knowledge of these codes is said to make one liberated while living.
location_in_parent: the latter 'four-hundred' of the Vāmakeśvara in Bhāskararāya's reckoning
